text: Clovis of the Merovingian line had defeated the last Roman governor in Gaul in 486 and united the Frankish subtribes. Around 498 he was baptized by Bishop Remigius at Reims, reportedly after a vow made in battle against the Alemanni. Because, unlike most Germanic kings, he chose the Catholic rather than the Arian confession, he won the support of the church and of the Roman population. After his victory over the Visigoths in 507 he ruled almost all of Gaul; his kingdom became the nucleus of France and Germany.

title: Tiwanaku on Lake Titicaca
summary: At an altitude of almost 4,000 meters, Tiwanaku becomes the religious and political center of the southern Andes.
text: Tiwanaku lay near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca in today's Bolivia. The city had temple platforms such as the Akapana, sunken courts and the famous Gateway of the Sun, which shows a deity holding two staffs. Around the city farmers laid out raised fields whose water channels protected the plants from night frost and allowed high yields. Llama caravans linked Tiwanaku with colonies on the Pacific coast and in the lowlands. A long drought probably contributed to the city's decline after 1000; for the Inca, Lake Titicaca remained a sacred place of origin.

title: Aksum's campaign to southern Arabia
summary: King Kaleb of Aksum crosses the Red Sea and conquers the kingdom of Himyar in present-day Yemen.
text: In the southern Arabian kingdom of Himyar, the Jewish king Yusuf As'ar, called Dhu Nuwas in Arabic sources, had the Christians of the city of Najran persecuted around 523. Kaleb of Aksum, who saw himself as protector of the Christians, then landed in Arabia with an army and defeated him. For several decades southern Arabia stood under Aksumite influence, later under the Aksumite commander Abraha, who made himself independent. The campaign shows how closely Aksum was bound up with the world beyond the Red Sea. Around 570 the region was lost to the Persian Sasanian Empire.

title: Benedict of Nursia Founds Monte Cassino
summary: With the monastery of Monte Cassino and his Rule, Benedict founds Western monasticism.
text: Benedict of Nursia had lived as a hermit near Subiaco before founding a monastery around 529 on the mountain of Cassino between Rome and Naples. For his community he wrote a Rule that divided the monks' day between prayer, reading and manual work, demanded moderation and obedience, and made the abbot the father of the community. Over the following centuries the Rule of Benedict prevailed in almost all monasteries of Western Europe. Monasteries such as Monte Cassino, Fulda, St. Gall and Cluny became centers of agriculture, nursing and the art of writing, where ancient manuscripts were preserved.

title: Justinian Consecrates the Hagia Sophia
summary: In Constantinople the largest church in the world is built in just five years, a symbol of the power of the Eastern Roman emperor Justinian.
text: After the Nika riot destroyed the old church in 532, Justinian had the mathematicians Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus build a structure with a seemingly floating dome more than 30 meters across. At the consecration on 27 December 537 he is said to have exclaimed that he had surpassed Solomon. In those same years Justinian had Roman law compiled in the Corpus Iuris Civilis, which shapes the legal order of Europe to this day, and with his generals Belisarius and Narses he reconquered North Africa and Italy. The Hagia Sophia was the largest church in Christendom for almost a thousand years, became a mosque in 1453 and is today a landmark of Istanbul.

title: The Wari empire
summary: From Ayacucho the Wari build the first great empire of the Andes.
text: The capital of the Wari lay near Ayacucho in the highlands of Peru. From there they dominated large parts of today's Peru between about 600 and 1000. They built planned administrative centers such as Pikillacta near Cusco, constructed roads and terraces and already used knotted cords for bookkeeping. Many researchers therefore see the Wari as forerunners of the Inca administration. Their art shares motifs such as the Staff God with Tiwanaku, with which they had both peaceful and hostile contact.

title: Muhammad's First Revelation
summary: In a cave on Mount Hira near Mecca, Muhammad receives the first revelation according to Islamic tradition.
text: Muhammad, a merchant of about forty from the Quraysh tribe, regularly withdrew to a cave on Mount Hira to reflect. There, according to Muslim belief, the angel Gabriel appeared to him with the charge to proclaim the words of God. The revelations he received until his death were later collected in the Quran. His preaching of the one God and of responsibility toward the poor and the weak won him his first followers but brought him into conflict with the leading families of Mecca, who profited from the worship of the old gods at the Kaaba.

title: Pakal rules at Palenque
summary: Under King Pakal, Palenque reaches its greatest flowering; his tomb is among the most important finds of Maya research.
text: Pakal ascended the throne of Palenque in 615 at the age of twelve, after his mother Sak K'uk' had ruled before him. During his reign of almost 70 years, the city recovered from defeats by Calakmul and became a leading kingdom in the west of the Maya region. He had the palace enlarged and the Temple of the Inscriptions built, whose texts tell the history of his dynasty. In 1952 Alberto Ruz Lhuillier discovered the burial chamber inside the pyramid with its richly carved sarcophagus and a death mask of jade.

title: The Beginning of the Tang Dynasty
summary: The Tang dynasty makes China the most powerful and most cosmopolitan empire of its time.
text: Li Yuan founded the Tang dynasty in 618, under which China was a cultural and political great power for almost three centuries. The capital Chang'an, with about a million inhabitants, hosted merchants, monks and envoys from Persia, India, Korea and Japan. The poets Li Bai and Du Fu, woodblock printing and the civil service examinations define the image of this period; in Wu Zetian, the only woman in Chinese history reigned as empress in her own right. After the rebellion of An Lushan from 755, the court gradually lost control of the provinces.

title: The Hijra to Medina
summary: Muhammad and his followers migrate from Mecca to Medina; the Islamic calendar begins with this year.
text: Because of growing hostility in Mecca, Muhammad and his companions accepted an invitation in 622 from the oasis of Yathrib, which from then on was called Medina, the city of the Prophet. There Muhammad became the religious and political head of a community that he bound to the resident tribes in a community charter. After several battles with the Meccans he returned to Mecca in 630 almost without a fight and dedicated the Kaaba to the one God. The caliph Umar later fixed the Hijra as the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

title: The Battle of Badr
summary: The small Muslim community from Medina defeats a considerably larger Meccan army at the oasis of Badr.
text: Two years after the Hijra, in March 624, the first great battle between Muhammad's followers and the leading families of Mecca took place at the oasis of Badr southwest of Medina. About 300 Muslims faced some 1,000 Meccans who had marched out to protect a trade caravan, and nevertheless won a clear victory in which several of their fiercest opponents fell. For the Muslims, Badr was a sign of divine support and considerably strengthened Muhammad's standing in Medina and among the tribes of Arabia. There followed the defeat at Uhud in 625 and the successful defense of Medina at the Battle of the Trench in 627, before Muhammad won Mecca in 630.

title: The Arab Conquest of Jerusalem
summary: The Byzantine city of Jerusalem surrenders to the caliph Umar, who guarantees protection to Christians and Jews.
text: After the victory over the Byzantines at the Yarmuk River in 636, Arab troops besieged Jerusalem, which the patriarch Sophronius handed over personally to the caliph Umar in 638. Umar guaranteed the Christians possession of their churches and once again allowed Jews, after centuries, to settle in the city. On the Temple Mount the Dome of the Rock was later built, completed in 691 and among the oldest Islamic structures. Jerusalem thus became a holy city of all three Abrahamic religions and remained under Muslim rule for more than 450 years.

title: The Baqt treaty between Makuria and Egypt
summary: The Christian Nubian kingdom of Makuria repels the Arab armies and concludes a treaty with Egypt that remains in force for about 600 years.
text: After the conquest of Egypt, Arab troops advanced up the Nile but in 652 failed in the siege of Dongola, the capital of Makuria, against the feared Nubian archers. Both sides then concluded the Baqt, a treaty of peace and exchange: Nubia delivered a fixed number of slaves each year, Egypt grain, cloth and other goods. The agreement secured Makuria centuries of independence as a Christian kingdom. Churches such as the cathedral of Faras with its colorful wall paintings bear witness to the flowering of Nubian culture. Only in the 14th century did the kingdom decline.

title: The Umayyad Caliphate in Damascus
summary: Muawiya founds the first caliphal dynasty and makes Damascus the capital of an empire reaching from Spain to the Indus.
text: After the murder of the fourth caliph Ali, the governor of Syria, Muawiya, prevailed and turned the caliphate into a hereditary office of his family. The dispute over the rightful succession to the Prophet led to the split into Sunnis and Shiites that persists to this day. Under the Umayyads, Arab armies conquered North Africa, in 711 the Visigothic kingdom in Spain, and territories as far as Central Asia and the Indus. Arabic became the language of administration, distinct gold coins were minted, and the Umayyad Mosque in Damascus was created as a masterpiece of Islamic architecture.

title: The Battle of Karbala
summary: Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, is killed with his companions by troops of the Umayyad caliph Yazid; the division between Sunnis and Shiites deepens.
text: After the death of the caliph Muawiya in 680, his son Yazid succeeded him, which many Muslims saw as a break with the election of the caliph. Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad and son of the fourth caliph Ali, set out with his family and a few dozen companions for Kufa in Iraq, where supporters had invited him to lead them. On 10 October 680 the small group was surrounded at Karbala by a vastly superior army, cut off from the water source and killed after a final fight. For the Shiites, the followers of Ali and his descendants, Husayn became a martyr; they commemorate his death every year on the day of Ashura, and Karbala is one of their most important places of pilgrimage.

title: Lady Six Sky renews the dynasty of Naranjo
summary: A princess from Dos Pilas comes to Naranjo and becomes the most powerful person in the kingdom.
text: In 682 Lady Six Sky, a daughter of the king of Dos Pilas, arrived at Naranjo, whose royal house had been weakened by defeats. Inscriptions celebrated her arrival as a new beginning for the dynasty. In 693 her five-year-old son was crowned king, but for years real power lay with her. Stelae show her in royal dress standing over captured enemies and report military campaigns in her time. She is one of the best-known female rulers of the Maya.

title: Wu Zetian Becomes Empress of China
summary: The emperor's former concubine proclaims a dynasty of her own and rules as the only woman in Chinese history to reign in her own right.
text: Wu Zetian was a concubine of two emperors and, after her husband Gaozong fell ill, directed the government from 660; after his death she stripped her sons of power. In 690 she had herself proclaimed emperor, founded the Zhou dynasty and based her rule on Buddhism, which celebrated her as the return of a bodhisattva. She promoted the civil service examinations, brought capable men from simple families into government, and expanded the empire toward Korea and Central Asia. In 705 a palace coup forced her, then over eighty, to abdicate, and the Tang dynasty was restored.

title: Tikal defeats Calakmul
summary: In the struggle between the two Maya great powers, Tikal wins a decisive victory over the Snake kingdom.
text: For more than a century Tikal and Calakmul, the Snake kingdom, struggled for supremacy in the Maya lowlands. In 562 Calakmul and its allies had defeated Tikal, after which no monuments were erected there for a long time. In 695 King Jasaw Chan K'awiil beat the army of the Calakmul king Yich'aak K'ahk' and celebrated the victory with festivals and carved wooden lintels. Calakmul never fully recovered, while Tikal enjoyed a new flowering. The wars show how strongly alliances and vassal relationships shaped Maya politics.

title: The Arab Siege of Constantinople
summary: A large Umayyad army and fleet besiege the Byzantine capital for a year but founder on its walls, on Greek fire and on the winter.
text: After conquering Syria, Egypt and North Africa, the Umayyads wanted to subdue Christian Byzantium as well, whose capital they had already besieged in vain from 674 to 678. In the summer of 717 the commander Maslama encircled Constantinople with a land army and hundreds of ships, and the new emperor Leo III defended it vigorously. Byzantine ships destroyed the Arab fleet with Greek fire, a burning liquid; an unusually harsh winter and epidemics decimated the besiegers, and the Bulgars attacked the Arab camp. In August 718 Maslama broke off the siege; Byzantium endured for another seven centuries and remained the barrier between the caliphate and southeastern Europe.

title: The Battle of Tours and Poitiers
summary: The Frankish mayor of the palace Charles Martel defeats an Arab-Berber army and halts the advance northward.
text: From Spain, Muslim armies repeatedly pushed across the Pyrenees into southern France. In October 732, Charles Martel confronted the governor Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi with his Frankish infantry between Tours and Poitiers; the Arab leader fell and his army withdrew. The significance of the battle was often exaggerated later, but it strengthened the position of the Carolingians, who gained the Frankish crown a few decades afterwards. Muslim rule remained confined to the Iberian Peninsula, where it lasted almost 800 more years.

title: The Abbasid Revolution
summary: A revolt from Khurasan overthrows the Umayyads; the Abbasids take over the caliphate and shift the empire's center eastward.
text: Umayyad rule was hated by many non-Arab Muslims, above all Persians, because despite their conversion to Islam they paid higher taxes and remained excluded from office; the Shiites and many pious Arabs rejected the dynasty as well. The Abbasids, descendants of an uncle of the Prophet, gathered these discontented groups, and in 747 troops rose under the commander Abu Muslim in Khurasan beneath black banners. In January 750 they defeated the Umayyad army at the Great Zab in Iraq, the last Umayyad caliph Marwan II was killed while fleeing in Egypt, and almost the entire family fell victim to a massacre. Only Abd al-Rahman escaped to Spain, where he founded the Emirate of Córdoba in 756. The Abbasids opened administration and court to Persians and other peoples and, with Baghdad, made Iraq the center of the Islamic world.

title: The Founding of Baghdad
summary: The Abbasid caliph al-Mansur founds a new capital on the Tigris that becomes the largest city in the world.
text: After the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads in 750, the caliph al-Mansur had a circular royal city built on the Tigris, which he called Madinat al-Salam, the City of Peace. Its favorable position on the trade routes between Persia, India, Arabia and the Mediterranean made Baghdad grow quickly; by around 900 more than half a million people probably lived there. Markets, libraries, hospitals and mosques made the city the center of the Islamic world. The tales of the Thousand and One Nights reflect the splendor of Abbasid Baghdad.

title: The Raid on Lindisfarne: the Beginning of the Viking Age
summary: Scandinavian seafarers plunder the monastery of Lindisfarne off the English coast and cause horror across Europe.
text: On 8 June 793, Vikings landed on the island of Lindisfarne, killed monks, stole church treasures and carried off captives. The attack is regarded as the beginning of the Viking Age, in which Northmen with their fast longships raided coasts and rivers from England to the Mediterranean. They were at the same time traders, explorers and settlers: they founded Dublin and Normandy, controlled trade routes to Russia and Byzantium, and around 1000 reached Iceland, Greenland and North America.

title: The Heian Period in Japan
summary: With the move of the capital to Heian-kyo, today's Kyoto, the classical court culture of Japan begins.
text: Emperor Kanmu moved the court to Heian-kyo in 794 to escape the influence of the powerful Buddhist monasteries of Nara. The noble Fujiwara family effectively governed in place of the emperors for centuries. At court the Japanese syllabaries were created, along with works such as The Tale of Genji by the lady-in-waiting Murasaki Shikibu, regarded as the first novel in world literature. When the warrior families of the Minamoto and the Taira fought for power, the era ended in 1185 with the establishment of the first shogunate.

title: The collapse of the Classic Maya cities
summary: In the 9th century the great royal cities in the southern Maya lowlands are abandoned.
text: From about 800 the inscriptions ceased in one city after another, palaces were abandoned and the population of the southern lowlands declined sharply. The last known Long Count date comes from Toniná in 909. Recurring droughts, overuse of soils and forests, constant wars and the loss of faith in the divine kings are considered causes. The Maya themselves did not vanish: in northern Yucatán cities such as Chichén Itzá continued to flourish, and millions of people still speak Maya languages today.

title: The Imperial Coronation of Charlemagne
summary: Pope Leo III crowns the Frankish king emperor in Rome on Christmas Day and renews the Western empire.
text: Charlemagne had built the Frankish kingdom through wars against Lombards, Saxons and Avars into the largest realm in Western Europe since Rome. When he protected Pope Leo III against his Roman opponents, the pope placed the imperial crown on his head in St. Peter's on 25 December 800. With that the West again claimed an empire of its own alongside Byzantium. Charlemagne reorganized administration, coinage and church, had schools founded and a new, easily legible script developed; this is known as the Carolingian Renaissance.

title: Al-Khwarizmi Founds Algebra
summary: The mathematician al-Khwarizmi writes a textbook in Baghdad on solving equations, from whose title the word algebra comes.
text: Around 820, Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi wrote at the court of the caliph al-Mamun The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing, in Arabic al-jabr wa'l-muqabala. In it he showed step by step how equations of the first and second degree can be solved, and explained their application to inheritance division, trade and land surveying; from al-jabr came the word algebra. In a second work he explained calculation with the Indian numerals and zero, which spread through Europe in Latin translation under his name as algorismus; from this came the term algorithm. Al-Khwarizmi also calculated astronomical tables and wrote a work of geography with the coordinates of more than 2,000 places.

title: The House of Wisdom in Baghdad
summary: Under the caliph al-Mamun, Baghdad becomes a center of translation and scholarship.
text: Harun al-Rashid had already built up a library in Baghdad; his son al-Mamun expanded it into an academy in which scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian writings into Arabic. The mathematician al-Khwarizmi wrote his textbook on calculating with equations here, from whose title the word algebra and from whose name the term algorithm arose. Astronomers measured the circumference of the Earth, and physicians such as Hunayn ibn Ishaq translated Galen and Hippocrates. The numerals with zero taken over from India spread from here throughout the Islamic world and later to Europe.

title: The Treaty of Verdun
summary: The grandsons of Charlemagne divide the Frankish empire into three parts; from West and East Francia, France and Germany emerge.
text: After the death of Louis the Pious in 840, his sons fought over the inheritance until they agreed on a partition at Verdun in 843: Charles the Bald received the west, Louis the German the east, and Lothair I, who held the imperial title, an elongated middle kingdom stretching from the North Sea to Italy. The year before, Charles and Louis had sworn their alliance in the Oaths of Strasbourg in Old French and Old High German, the oldest surviving texts in either language. The middle kingdom soon broke apart and remained a bone of contention between its neighbors into the 20th century, while the East and West Frankish kingdoms developed into Germany and France.

title: The rise of Chichén Itzá
summary: In northern Yucatán, Chichén Itzá becomes the leading city of the Maya world.
text: While the cities of the south declined, Chichén Itzá rose to dominance in the north of the Yucatán peninsula. Its landmark is the pyramid of Kukulkan, the feathered serpent, on whose staircase a play of shadows resembling a serpent's body appears at the equinoxes. The city has the largest ball court in Mesoamerica and a sacred cenote, a natural well into which offerings of gold, jade and human beings were thrown. Architectural forms and images resemble those of Tula and show close contacts with central Mexico. Later Mayapán took over the leadership in Yucatán.

title: The great houses of Chaco Canyon
summary: The Ancestral Puebloans build multistory structures and a wide network of roads in southwestern North America.
text: In Chaco Canyon in present-day New Mexico, large multistory stone buildings were erected between about 850 and 1150. The largest, Pueblo Bonito, had hundreds of rooms and round ceremonial chambers, the kivas. Straight roads led to outlying settlements, and finds of turquoise, macaws and cacao bear witness to trade reaching as far as Mesoamerica. After a long drought Chaco lost its importance; later the cliff dwellings of Mesa Verde arose, which were likewise abandoned around 1300. The descendants of the builders live today among the Hopi, Zuni and other Pueblo peoples.

title: The Diamond Sutra: the oldest dated printed book
summary: A Buddhist text is printed from woodblocks in China; it is still regarded as the oldest dated printed work in the world.
text: The Diamond Sutra is a scroll five meters long, made of seven sheets pasted together, whose closing note records that a certain Wang Jie had it made on 11 May 868 in memory of his parents. Text and a frontispiece were cut in mirror image into wooden blocks, inked, and pressed onto paper; the technique had been in use in China since the 7th century for amulets and calendars. The scroll lay for more than a thousand years in a walled-up cave near Dunhuang, until the explorer Aurel Stein acquired it in 1907; today it is kept in the British Library. In the 11th century Bi Sheng in China also invented movable type made of clay.

title: Chan Chan, the capital of the Chimú
summary: On the north coast of Peru the largest adobe city in the Americas arises.
text: The kingdom of Chimor, whose inhabitants are called Chimú, dominated a long stretch of Peru's coast from the 10th to the 15th century. Its capital Chan Chan near Trujillo was built of adobe bricks and covered many square kilometers. High walls enclosed large palace compounds of the kings with courtyards, storerooms and burial platforms, decorated with reliefs of fish, birds and waves. The Chimú were famous metalworkers and built extensive irrigation systems. Around 1470 the Inca conquered the kingdom and brought its goldsmiths to Cusco.

title: Tula, the city of the Toltecs
summary: North of the Valley of Mexico, Tula becomes the center of the Toltecs, whom the Aztecs later regarded as exemplary ancestors.
text: After the decline of Teotihuacan, Tula in today's state of Hidalgo became the most important city of central Mexico. On a temple pyramid the stone warrior figures more than four meters tall, the so-called Atlanteans, still stand today. Reliefs with jaguars, eagles and skull racks show the importance of war and sacrifice. Around 1150 the city was destroyed or abandoned. The Aztecs later glorified the Toltecs as the inventors of all the arts and derived the dignity of their own rulers from them.

title: Caliphate of Córdoba
summary: Abd al-Rahman III proclaims himself caliph in Spain and makes Córdoba the most splendid city in Europe.
text: After the fall of the Umayyads in Damascus, a fugitive of the dynasty had founded an emirate of his own in Spain. In 929 Abd al-Rahman III assumed the title of caliph, placing himself on a par with the Abbasids in Baghdad and the Fatimids in North Africa. Córdoba had paved and lighted streets, baths, hundreds of mosques, and a library said to hold 400,000 volumes; in the palace city of Madinat al-Zahra the caliph received envoys from Byzantium and the Frankish empire. Muslims, Jews, and Christians long lived together in al-Andalus in relative peace. In 1031 the caliphate broke apart into numerous small kingdoms.

title: Otto I triumphs at the Lechfeld
summary: The East Frankish king defeats the Hungarians near Augsburg and is crowned emperor seven years later.
text: Since the end of the 9th century, mounted Hungarian warriors had plundered central Europe almost every year. When they besieged Augsburg in 955, which Bishop Ulrich was defending, Otto I led an army drawn from all the tribes of the realm against them on 10 August and won a complete victory at the Lechfeld. The Hungarians then settled permanently in the Pannonian plain and adopted Christianity around 1000. Otto's standing was now so great that Pope John XII crowned him emperor in Rome in 962; this was the beginning of the Holy Roman Empire, which lasted until 1806.

title: The Fatimids found Cairo and al-Azhar
summary: The Shiite Fatimids conquer Egypt, found the royal city of al-Qahira, and build the al-Azhar mosque as a place of learning.
text: The Fatimids, a Shiite dynasty that traced its descent from Fatima, the daughter of the Prophet, had established a caliphate of their own in North Africa in 909. In 969 their general Jawhar conquered Egypt and had a new palace city laid out north of the old capital Fustat, which was given the name al-Qahira, the victorious; from this came Cairo. From 970 the al-Azhar mosque was built there, where jurists and theologians soon taught; it is regarded as one of the oldest universities still in existence. Under the Fatimids, Cairo became the richest center of the Islamic world, with libraries, markets, and trade across the Red Sea to India; after the dynasty ended in 1171, Saladin made al-Azhar a Sunni institution of learning, which it remains to this day.

title: Rise of the Chola empire in South India
summary: Under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I, the Cholas become the leading land and sea power of the Indian Ocean.
text: Rajaraja I ascended the Chola throne in the Tamil south of India in 985, subdued the neighboring kingdoms and Sri Lanka, and had the enormous Brihadishvara temple to Shiva built at Thanjavur. His son Rajendra I sent an army as far as the Ganges and, in 1025, a fleet against the kingdom of Srivijaya on Sumatra in order to control the sea routes to China. The Cholas governed their empire through village assemblies whose decisions are recorded in temple inscriptions, and their bronze sculptors created the dancing Shiva Nataraja, a masterpiece of world art. The empire broke apart in the 13th century.

title: Christianization of Kievan Rus
summary: Grand Prince Vladimir is baptized and makes Orthodox Christianity the religion of his realm on the Dnieper.
text: Kievan Rus had emerged in the 9th century from Scandinavian merchant-warriors, the Varangians, and Slavic tribes, and it controlled the trade route from the Baltic to Byzantium. Vladimir I was baptized in 988, married Anna, the sister of the Byzantine emperor Basil II, and had the population of Kiev baptized in the Dnieper. With the faith came the Cyrillic script, canon law, icon painting, and master builders from Byzantium; under Yaroslav the Wise the Cathedral of Saint Sophia in Kiev and the first law code were created. Rus thus became the cradle of Russian, Ukrainian, and Belarusian culture, until the Mongols destroyed Kiev in 1240.

title: Murasaki Shikibu completes The Tale of Genji
summary: At the Japanese imperial court, a lady-in-waiting writes the story of Prince Genji, regarded as the first novel in world literature.
text: Murasaki Shikibu served Empress Shoshi at the court of Heian-kyo, where she wrote the story of Prince Genji, his love affairs, and his descendants in 54 chapters, using the Japanese syllabary. Her diary mentions the work for the first time in 1008, when parts of it were already being read aloud at court. With a fine feeling for emotion, the seasons, and transience, the novel depicts the courtly world of the Heian period, and in Japan it was copied, illustrated, and annotated for centuries. At the same time her rival Sei Shonagon wrote The Pillow Book, a collection of observations and lists.

title: The Song dynasty: gunpowder, compass, and paper money
summary: The first recipe for gunpowder is recorded in Song China in 1044; the compass, paper money, and movable type follow in the same century.
text: The Song dynasty, founded in 960, ruled an economically flourishing China with cities of a million people such as Kaifeng and Hangzhou. In 1044 the military manual Wujing Zongyao described for the first time mixtures of saltpeter, sulfur, and charcoal for fire arrows and bombs; fire lances and explosive bombs followed in the 12th century. In 1088 the scholar Shen Kuo recorded how a magnetized needle points south, and Chinese seafarers soon used the compass for navigation. The state issued the world's first paper money, Bi Sheng invented movable type, and iron production reached quantities that Europe did not match again until the 18th century.

title: Cahokia, center of the Mississippian culture
summary: On the Mississippi the largest settlement in North America north of Mexico arises.
text: Opposite present-day St. Louis, Cahokia grew around 1050 into a city of probably 10,000 to 20,000 inhabitants. Its basis was maize farming in the fertile river floodplain. More than a hundred earthen mounds carried temples, elite houses and graves; the largest, Monks Mound, is about 30 meters high and the largest earthwork in North America. Circles of wooden posts probably served as solar calendars. Cahokia shaped the Mississippian culture throughout the Southeast, but lost inhabitants from about 1200 and was largely abandoned by 1350.

title: Battle of Hastings
summary: Duke William of Normandy defeats the Anglo-Saxon king Harold and conquers England.
text: After the death of the childless king Edward the Confessor, William claimed the English throne, which Harold Godwinson had, however, already taken. On 14 October 1066 the armies met near Hastings; Harold fell in the fighting, and William had himself crowned at Westminster at Christmas. The Norman Conquest brought to England a French-speaking nobility, castles of stone, the feudal system, and a tight administration, recorded in the Domesday Book of 1086. The Bayeux Tapestry tells the events across seventy meters of cloth.

title: Al-Bakri describes the empire of Ghana
summary: The geographer al-Bakri in Córdoba portrays the West African gold empire of Ghana and its court.
text: The empire of Ghana, called Wagadu by its inhabitants, the Soninke, lay in the border region of the present-day states of Mauritania and Mali. It controlled the trade between the goldfields in the south and the caravans from North Africa that brought salt and goods across the Sahara. The scholar al-Bakri, who never went there himself, collected merchants' reports in Córdoba and in 1068 described a capital in two parts: a town of Muslim traders with twelve mosques and the royal town with sacred groves. The king ruled with great splendor and levied duties on every load of salt. His account is one of the most important sources on the first great empire of West Africa.

title: The Seljuks win at Manzikert
summary: Sultan Alp Arslan defeats the Byzantine army and takes Emperor Romanos IV prisoner; Anatolia becomes Turkish and Islamic.
text: The Seljuks, a Turkic nomadic people from Central Asia, had adopted Sunni Islam, taken Baghdad in 1055, and placed the Abbasid caliph under their protection; from then on their ruler bore the title of sultan. On 26 August 1071 Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes faced Alp Arslan's army at Manzikert in eastern Anatolia, was defeated by the cavalry tactics of the Turks, and was taken captive. Alp Arslan released him for a ransom, but civil wars broke out in Byzantium, and Turkish tribes advanced almost unhindered into Asia Minor, where the Sultanate of Rum arose with its capital at Konya. The Byzantine emperor's appeal to the pope for help was one of the reasons for the First Crusade in 1096.

title: The Investiture Controversy and the road to Canossa
summary: King Henry IV stands as a penitent before the castle of Canossa and asks Pope Gregory VII to lift his excommunication.
text: Pope Gregory VII had forbidden rulers to install bishops in office with ring and staff, because he wanted to free the church from secular power. When Henry IV responded in 1076 by declaring the pope deposed, Gregory pronounced the ban on the king and released his subjects from their oath of loyalty. Pressed by the princes, Henry crossed the Alps in winter and waited for three days in January 1077 in penitential dress before the castle of Canossa, until Gregory received him back into the church. The conflict continued for decades and was ended only in 1122 by a compromise in the Concordat of Worms.

title: The ruler of Kanem converts to Islam
summary: With King Hume, a ruler of the empire of Kanem on Lake Chad becomes a Muslim for the first time.
text: The empire of Kanem lay northeast of Lake Chad and lived from trade along the caravan route to Fezzan and Libya, on which mainly slaves, ivory and horses were traded. According to tradition, King Hume converted to Islam in the late 11th century and founded the Sayfawa dynasty. This ruling family reigned until 1846 and thus ranks among the longest-lasting dynasties in world history. In the 14th century the kings moved their seat to Bornu, west of the lake, which is why historians speak of the empire of Kanem-Bornu. Several rulers made the pilgrimage to Mecca and maintained relations as far as Egypt.

title: Founding of the University of Bologna
summary: Europe's first university grows out of the law schools of Bologna; Paris and Oxford follow in the 12th century.
text: In Bologna scholars such as Irnerius had specialized in the rediscovered Roman law of Justinian and attracted students from all over Europe. Around 1088 these students joined together in corporations that hired professors and regulated teaching; the word university originally denoted this community of teachers and learners. Emperor Frederick Barbarossa placed the scholars under his protection in 1155, and the popes gave their degrees validity throughout Christendom. By 1500 there were around 70 universities, among them Paris, Oxford, Salamanca, Prague, Vienna, and Heidelberg.

title: The First Crusade and the capture of Jerusalem
summary: At the pope's call, knights from all over Europe march to the Holy Land and capture Jerusalem.
text: At the Synod of Clermont in 1095, Pope Urban II called for help for the Byzantine Christians and for the liberation of the holy sites from Muslim rule. Tens of thousands answered the call, among them knights under Godfrey of Bouillon and Raymond of Toulouse. After a costly march through Asia Minor and the siege of Antioch, the crusaders took Jerusalem on 15 July 1099 and carried out a massacre of the population. They founded several crusader states, which held out for almost two centuries; six more major crusades followed.

title: The beginning of Gothic architecture at Saint-Denis
summary: Abbot Suger has a light-filled choir built near Paris and with it establishes the style of the Gothic cathedrals.
text: In 1140 Abbot Suger began rebuilding the abbey church of Saint-Denis, the burial place of the French kings, combining pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and large stained-glass windows into a new whole. Because the weight of the vaults was carried from outside by buttresses, the walls could be made thin and the light, which for Suger was an image of God, could enter unhindered. Within a few decades the cathedrals of Chartres, Paris, Reims, and Amiens were built on this model, and in 1248 construction of Cologne Cathedral began. With their towers, sculptures, and rose windows, the Gothic cathedrals were the tallest buildings of their time and an expression of the pride of the growing cities.

title: Construction of Angkor Wat
summary: The Khmer build the largest temple complex in the world in present-day Cambodia.
text: In the first half of the 12th century, King Suryavarman II had Angkor Wat built as a temple to the Hindu god Vishnu and as his own tomb. Surrounded by moats, the complex with its five towers reproduces Mount Meru, the world mountain of Hindu cosmology, and is decorated with reliefs kilometers long. The Khmer empire then ruled large parts of Southeast Asia and supplied its capital by means of an ingenious canal system. Angkor Wat later became a Buddhist sanctuary and is today the national symbol of Cambodia.

title: Ibn Rushd explains Aristotle in Córdoba
summary: At the request of the Almohad caliph, the judge and physician Ibn Rushd begins his commentaries on Aristotle, which change the thought of Europe.
text: Around 1169 the Almohad caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf commissioned the scholar Ibn Rushd of Córdoba to explain the difficult writings of Aristotle. Over the following decades Ibn Rushd wrote commentaries on almost all the works of the Greek philosopher and, in a treatise of his own, defended the compatibility of reason and revelation against the criticism of the theologian al-Ghazali. In 1195 he fell out of favor for a time because of his philosophy and had to go into exile. His commentaries were translated into Latin and Hebrew as early as the 13th century; at the University of Paris he was known simply as the Commentator, and Thomas Aquinas engaged with him intensively.

title: Saladin retakes Jerusalem
summary: After his victory at Hattin, Saladin takes the city again almost nine decades after the First Crusade.
text: Saladin had united Egypt and Syria under his rule and called for war against the crusader states. On 4 July 1187, at the Horns of Hattin, he destroyed the army of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, which was cut off from water in the summer heat. On 2 October Jerusalem capitulated; unlike the crusaders in 1099, Saladin spared the inhabitants and let them leave on payment of a ransom. The loss of the city set off the Third Crusade, in which Richard the Lionheart did win back Acre, but Jerusalem remained in Muslim hands.

title: Minamoto no Yoritomo becomes shogun
summary: The victor of the Genpei War receives the title of shogun from the emperor and establishes Japan's first warrior government in Kamakura.
text: In the Genpei War of 1180 to 1185 the warrior clan of the Minamoto defeated their rivals, the Taira. Their leader Yoritomo set up his government not at the imperial court in Kyoto but in Kamakura in eastern Japan, and in 1192 received the title of shogun. This began a period of almost 700 years in which military governments ruled the country while the emperor performed mainly ceremonial duties. After Yoritomo's death the family of his widow Hōjō Masako took over the leadership as regents.

title: The flourishing of Great Zimbabwe
summary: In southern Africa the ancestors of the Shona build a stone city that lives from the gold trade with the Swahili coast.
text: Between the 11th and 15th centuries a city of up to 18,000 inhabitants arose on the plateau of present-day Zimbabwe, its rulers controlling cattle herds and gold deposits. Its walls of carefully layered granite blocks, set without mortar, reach eleven meters in height; the Great Enclosure with its conical tower is the largest precolonial structure south of the Sahara. Finds of Chinese porcelain, Persian ceramics, and Arab coins show that gold and ivory were traded through ports such as Kilwa and Sofala as far as India and China. The city was abandoned around 1450; colonial researchers long disputed the African origin of the buildings, which today give the state of Zimbabwe its name and its emblem.

title: The bronze heads of Ife
summary: In the sacred Yoruba city of Ife, naturalistic heads of copper alloy and terracotta of great artistry are created.
text: In Yoruba tradition, Ife in the southwest of present-day Nigeria is the place where the world was created and the place of origin of their royal families. Between the 12th and 15th centuries artists there made life-size heads of copper alloys using the lost-wax technique, as well as of fired clay. The faces are so lifelike that European researchers such as Leo Frobenius at first refused to believe they were African works. They probably depicted kings and dignitaries and were used in rituals. The art of Ife influenced the later casters in the kingdom of Benin.

title: The rock-hewn churches of Lalibela
summary: Under King Lalibela, eleven churches are carved entirely out of the living rock in the Ethiopian highlands.
text: Lalibela belonged to the Zagwe dynasty, which ruled Christian Ethiopia after the decline of Aksum. Around 1200, in the town later named after him, eleven churches were created that were not built of masonry but carved downwards out of the volcanic rock. The most famous, Bete Giyorgis, has the ground plan of a cross and stands in a deep pit. According to tradition, the complex was meant to represent a new Jerusalem after pilgrimage to the Holy Land had become difficult. The churches are still the destination of countless pilgrims and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: The Taíno chiefdoms of the Caribbean
summary: On the Greater Antilles the Taíno develop a society with caciques, ball courts and ancestral figures.
text: The ancestors of the Taíno had migrated from South America along the island chain of the Lesser Antilles. By around 1200 a society with hereditary chiefs, the caciques, among them women, had developed on Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, Cuba and Jamaica. The Taíno grew cassava on heaped-up earth mounds, traveled between the islands in large dugout canoes and played a ball game on plazas lined with stones, the bateyes. They venerated spirits and ancestors in figures called zemís. Words such as canoe, hammock, hurricane and tobacco come from their language.

title: Genghis Khan unites the Mongols
summary: Temüjin is proclaimed ruler of all the Mongol tribes and begins to build a world empire.
text: At an assembly of the tribes on the Onon River in 1206, Temüjin received the title Genghis Khan, which means roughly oceanic or universal ruler. He organized the Mongols into units of ten, a hundred, and a thousand warriors, introduced a law code, and promoted men by achievement rather than by birth. His mounted archers conquered northern China, Central Asia, and Persia; his successors extended the empire as far as Eastern Europe and southern China. Despite the brutality of their warfare, the Pax Mongolica later secured trade along the Silk Road.

title: Founding of the Delhi Sultanate
summary: After the death of his master Muhammad of Ghor, the commander Qutb ud-Din Aibak makes himself independent in Delhi and founds the first lasting Muslim state in northern India.
text: Qutb ud-Din Aibak had risen as a military slave and had conquered large parts of northern India for Muhammad of Ghor. He had already begun the Quwwat al-Islam mosque and the Qutb Minar minaret in Delhi; after his master's death in 1206 he ruled as an independent sovereign. The sultanate was ruled in turn by five dynasties and repelled several Mongol attacks in the 13th and 14th centuries. From 1236 to 1240 a woman, Radiyya, even ruled as sultan. In 1526 Babur defeated the last sultan at Panipat.

title: Magna Carta
summary: English barons force King John to acknowledge their rights in a charter.
text: King John Lackland had turned the nobility against him through lost wars in France and heavy levies. On 15 June 1215, in the meadow of Runnymede, he had to set his seal to Magna Carta, which laid down among other things that no free man may be imprisoned without lawful judgment and that no tax may be levied without the consent of the council. The charter at first applied only to the nobility and was soon annulled again, yet it was confirmed over and over and became a symbol of the ruler's subjection to the law.

title: Sundiata wins at Kirina and founds Mali
summary: The Mande prince Sundiata Keita defeats the Sosso king Sumanguru and lays the foundation of the Mali Empire.
text: After the decline of Ghana, the Sosso king Sumanguru Kante had subjugated the lands on the upper Niger. Sundiata Keita, a Malinke prince, rallied the Mande peoples against him and defeated him around 1235 in the battle of Kirina. He then became the founder of the Mali Empire, which in the following decades expanded from the Atlantic to the bend of the Niger and controlled the goldfields of Bambuk and Bure. His life is known above all through the epic of Sundiata, which griots still perform today. Rules for the coexistence of the clans, known in oral tradition as the Kurukan Fuga charter, were also traced back to him.

title: The Mongol invasion of Eastern Europe
summary: Mongol armies under Batu conquer the Russian principalities, destroy Kyiv and win victories in 1241 at Legnica and on the Sajó river in Hungary.
text: From 1237 the Mongols under Batu, a grandson of Genghis Khan, attacked the divided principalities of Rus and took one city after another. Kyiv fell in December 1240, and in April 1241 Mongol armies defeated a Silesian-Polish force at Legnica and the Hungarian army at Mohi on the Sajó. After the death of the Great Khan Ögedei they withdrew unexpectedly in 1242. On the Volga Batu founded the Golden Horde, to which the Russian princes paid tribute for more than two centuries.

title: The Mongols destroy Baghdad
summary: Hülegü's army captures and plunders Baghdad and brings the Abbasid caliphate to an end.
text: The Mongol prince Hülegü, a grandson of Genghis Khan, marched on Baghdad with an enormous army after its caliph al-Mustasim had refused to submit. After a short siege the city fell in February 1258; tens of thousands of inhabitants were killed, palaces, mosques, and libraries were destroyed, and the caliph was executed. The end of the Abbasid caliphate and the devastation of the irrigation system in Mesopotamia struck the Islamic world hard. In 1260 the Mamluks of Egypt halted the Mongol advance at Ain Jalut in Palestine; a few decades later the Mongol rulers of Persia themselves adopted Islam.

title: Beginning of the Solomonic dynasty in Ethiopia
summary: Yekuno Amlak overthrows the Zagwe kings and founds a dynasty that traces its origin back to King Solomon.
text: Yekuno Amlak, a lord from the province of Amhara, ended the rule of the Zagwe dynasty in 1270. His successors justified their power with the legend that they descended from Menelik, the son of King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. In the 14th century this story was written down at length in the Kebra Nagast, the Book of the Glory of Kings. The Solomonic dynasty ruled, with interruptions, until 1974, when Emperor Haile Selassie was overthrown. It bound the monarchy closely to the Ethiopian church.

title: Kublai Khan founds the Yuan dynasty
summary: The Mongol ruler Kublai Khan proclaims a dynasty on the Chinese model and by 1279 unites all of China under Mongol rule.
text: Kublai, a grandson of Genghis Khan, had made himself Great Khan in 1260 after a war with his brother. In 1271 he gave his rule in China the Chinese dynastic name Yuan and made Dadu, present-day Beijing, his capital. By 1279 he had conquered the Southern Song empire and reunited China for the first time in centuries. The Mongols divided the population into ranked classes in which the southern Chinese stood at the very bottom. The Yuan promoted trade and paper money but were overthrown by uprisings in 1368.

title: Marco Polo's journey to China
summary: The young Venetian travels with his father and uncle along the Silk Road to the court of the Mongol ruler Kublai Khan.
text: In 1271 the seventeen-year-old Marco Polo set out from Venice with his father Niccolò and his uncle Maffeo, and after almost four years reached the residence of Kublai Khan in China. By his own account he spent some seventeen years in the service of the Great Khan and traveled through large parts of East Asia before returning by sea in 1295. In Genoese captivity he dictated his experiences, which became known as Il Milione. The account of paper money, coal, and huge cities shaped the European picture of Asia and later inspired Columbus.

title: The Mongol invasions of Japan
summary: Two invasion fleets sent by Kublai Khan fail against the Japanese defences and violent storms, which are revered in Japan as kamikaze, the divine wind.
text: After Japan had refused to submit, a Mongol-Korean army landed in Hakata Bay on Kyūshū in 1274 but withdrew after fighting and a storm. The government in Kamakura then had a defensive wall built along the coast. In 1281 an even larger fleet came from Korea and southern China and, after weeks of fighting, was largely destroyed by a typhoon. The Japanese saw this as the protection of the gods. However, the cost of the defence weakened the Kamakura shogunate, which fell in 1333.

title: Founding of the Ottoman Empire
summary: The Turkish prince Osman makes himself independent in northwestern Anatolia and founds a dynasty that will rule for six centuries.
text: After the collapse of the Sultanate of Rum, numerous Turkish principalities arose in Anatolia. On the border with Byzantium, Osman I led warriors who saw themselves as fighters for the faith, and step by step he conquered Byzantine cities. His son Orhan took Bursa in 1326 and made it the first capital; in 1354 the Ottomans crossed into Europe. Within 150 years they had conquered the Balkans and Constantinople and had become the leading power of the Islamic world, one that lasted until 1922.

title: The flourishing of the Swahili city of Kilwa
summary: Through the gold trade, the island city of Kilwa on the coast of present-day Tanzania becomes the richest trading city in East Africa.
text: Kilwa Kisiwani controlled the trade in gold from the Zimbabwe plateau, which reached the coast through the port of Sofala. Its sultans minted their own copper coins and in the early 14th century had the Great Mosque enlarged and the palace of Husuni Kubwa built. Ibn Battuta visited the city around 1331 and praised it as one of the most beautiful cities in the world. Merchants from Arabia, Persia and India brought cloth, beads and Chinese porcelain. In 1505 the Portuguese conquered and plundered Kilwa, and the city never recovered.

title: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca
summary: The king of the Mali empire crosses the Sahara to Mecca with an enormous caravan and tons of gold.
text: Mansa Musa ruled the Mali empire, which with the gold mines of the western Sudan and the trading cities of Timbuktu and Gao was among the richest states in the world. On his pilgrimage in 1324 he was accompanied, according to contemporary reports, by thousands of people and camels loaded with gold, which he gave away so freely in Cairo that the price of gold there fell for years. On the way back he brought scholars and master builders with him and had mosques and schools built in Timbuktu. The Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows him holding a nugget of gold as the ruler of West Africa.

title: The travels of Ibn Battuta
summary: A Moroccan jurist crosses the entire Islamic world from West Africa to China in almost thirty years.
text: Ibn Battuta set out from Tangier in 1325 on the pilgrimage to Mecca and then traveled on: to East Africa, Anatolia, the court of the Golden Horde, and India, where he served for years as a judge to the sultan of Delhi, and on to the Maldives, Sumatra, and China. After his return he also visited al-Andalus and the Mali empire in West Africa. In all he covered around 120,000 kilometers, far more than Marco Polo. His travel account, the Rihla, is one of the most important sources on society, trade, and everyday life in the Islamic world of the 14th century.

title: Founding of Tenochtitlan by the Aztecs
summary: The Mexica found the city that becomes the capital of the Aztec empire on an island in Lake Texcoco.
text: According to tradition, the Mexica settled where they saw an eagle on a cactus, as their god Huitzilopochtli had foretold; that image adorns the flag of Mexico today. Through causeways, floating gardens, and canals, the island settlement grew into a city of more than 200,000 inhabitants, with huge temple pyramids and markets. From 1428 Tenochtitlan, in a triple alliance with Texcoco and Tlacopan, ruled large parts of Mexico and demanded tribute and captives for human sacrifice. In 1521 the Spaniards under Cortés conquered the city; Mexico City arose on its ruins.

title: Timbuktu becomes a center of trade and scholarship
summary: Under the Mali empire, the caravan city on the Niger develops into a center of the gold trade and of Islamic scholarship.
text: Timbuktu had come into being around 1100 as a camping place of Tuareg nomads on the edge of the Sahara, where caravans carrying salt from the desert met boats from the Niger carrying gold, ivory, and slaves. After his pilgrimage to Mecca, Mansa Musa brought back the Andalusian architect Abu Ishaq al-Sahili in 1325, who built the great Djinguereber Mosque out of mud brick; at the Sankoré Mosque and in private houses, schools arose in which scholars from North Africa and Egypt taught law, grammar, astronomy, and medicine. In the 15th and 16th centuries, under the Songhai empire, Timbuktu was one of the most important centers of learning in Africa, with thousands of students and a lively trade in manuscripts. Tens of thousands of these manuscripts survive to this day and refute the prejudice that Africa south of the Sahara had no written culture.

title: Orhan conquers Bursa
summary: After a long siege the Ottomans take the Byzantine city of Bursa and make it their first capital.
text: Osman's warriors had blockaded Bursa at the foot of Mount Uludağ from fortresses for years until the starving city surrendered to his son Orhan in 1326. Osman died around this time and was buried in Bursa. Orhan made the city his capital, had mosques, baths and caravanserais built, and soon also conquered Nicaea (1331) and Nicomedia (1337). Bursa became a centre of the silk trade between Persia and Europe and remained the burial place of the early sultans.

title: Founding of the Vijayanagara Empire
summary: The brothers Harihara and Bukka found a Hindu empire in southern India whose capital becomes one of the largest cities in the world.
text: According to tradition, around 1336 the brothers Harihara and Bukka founded the city of Vijayanagara, the City of Victory, on the Tungabhadra river. The empire soon dominated all of southern India and was in constant rivalry with the Muslim sultanates of the Deccan. Under King Krishnadevaraya it reached its height in the early 16th century; Portuguese visitors described the capital as magnificent and as large as Rome. In 1565 its army was defeated at Talikota by an alliance of the sultanates, and the capital was plundered. Its ruins at Hampi are now a World Heritage Site.

title: The Hundred Years' War
summary: England and France struggle for more than a century over the French throne and the territories in western France.
text: The war began when the English king Edward III, as the grandson of a French king, claimed the crown of France. English longbowmen won at Crécy in 1346, Poitiers in 1356, and Agincourt in 1415, and for a time France was close to falling apart. In 1429 Joan of Arc turned the tide by relieving Orléans and led the Dauphin to his coronation at Reims. With the battle of Castillon in 1453, England lost all its possessions on the mainland except Calais; both countries emerged from the war with a stronger sense of nationhood and with standing armies.

title: The Black Death
summary: The plague spreads along trade routes across the whole of Europe and kills about a third of the population.
text: In the autumn of 1347 Genoese ships from the Crimea brought the plague to Messina, from where it spread within four years across Italy, France, England, Germany, and Scandinavia. The pathogen Yersinia pestis was transmitted by fleas from rats and was incurable; whole villages died out. Many looked for someone to blame and murdered Jews in numerous cities. The catastrophe led to a shortage of labor, rising wages, peasant revolts, and a new view of death and transience in art and religion.

title: The heyday of the Alhambra in Granada
summary: The Nasrid sultans build the Alhambra palace city in Granada, the most magnificent structure of Islamic Spain.
text: After the Christian kingdoms had conquered Córdoba and Seville in the 13th century, the Emirate of Granada remained as the last Muslim state on the Iberian Peninsula and paid tribute to Castile. On a hill above the city, the Nasrid sultans expanded the Alhambra, the red fortress, into a fortified palace city; its finest parts, such as the Comares Palace and the Court of the Lions, were built around the middle of the 14th century under Yusuf I and Muhammad V. Stucco ornament, calligraphy with verses from the Quran and with poems, colored tiles, wooden ceilings, and gardens threaded with water make the complex a high point of Islamic art. After 1492 the Spanish monarchs continued to use the Alhambra, so that it survived almost unchanged and today belongs to the World Heritage.

title: Founding of Ayutthaya
summary: King Ramathibodi I founds the city of Ayutthaya on a river island; it remains the capital of the Siamese kingdom for more than 400 years.
text: Ayutthaya lay on an island in the Chao Phraya river and was easily reached from the sea. From here the kings ruled large parts of present-day Thailand and in 1431 captured Angkor, the capital of the Khmer. Chinese, Persian, Japanese and European merchants settled in their own quarters, and the city became one of the most important trading centres in Southeast Asia. Theravada Buddhism shaped the court and its culture. In 1767 Burmese troops captured and destroyed the city; the new capital later became Bangkok.

title: The Ottomans gain a foothold in Europe
summary: After an earthquake Ottoman troops occupy the fortress of Gallipoli on the Dardanelles and begin the conquest of the Balkans.
text: In the Byzantine civil war Ottoman mercenaries had fought for Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos, who married his daughter Theodora to Orhan. When an earthquake destroyed the walls of Gallipoli in March 1354, Orhan's son Süleyman Pasha occupied the town and stayed. From this bridgehead Turkish warriors advanced into Thrace, where settlers from Anatolia made their homes. In the 1360s Adrianople fell and, as Edirne, became the new capital.

title: First Hanseatic Diet in Lübeck
summary: The merchants and cities of the Hanseatic League meet for the first time in a joint assembly and become the trading power of the north.
text: From the 12th century onward, Low German merchants had joined together in associations in order to obtain protection and privileges abroad; trading posts in London, Bruges, Bergen, and Novgorod were their bases. In 1356 the representatives of the cities gathered for the first time in Lübeck for a Hanseatic Diet, which passed joint resolutions on trade, law, and war. At its height some 200 cities from Cologne to Reval belonged to the League, which in the Peace of Stralsund in 1370 even forced the king of Denmark into far-reaching concessions. With the rise of the Dutch and of the territorial princes, the League lost importance in the 16th century; the last Hanseatic Diet was held in 1669.

title: Founding of the Ming dynasty
summary: The rebel peasant's son Zhu Yuanzhang proclaims himself emperor in Nanjing and drives the Mongols out of China.
text: Famines, floods and heavy taxation led in the 1350s to great uprisings against the Yuan, above all the Red Turban movement. Zhu Yuanzhang, who as an orphan had lived in a Buddhist monastery, prevailed over the other rebel leaders. In 1368 he proclaimed the Ming dynasty in Nanjing, his troops took Dadu, and the last Yuan emperor fled to Mongolia. As the Hongwu emperor he had the land surveyed, villages reorganized and thousands of alleged conspirators executed. The Ming ruled China until 1644.

title: The conquests of Timur
summary: From Samarkand, Timur subdues Persia, India, Syria, and Anatolia and makes his capital a center of art and learning.
text: Timur, a Turco-Mongol warlord from what is now Uzbekistan, seized power in Samarkand in 1370 and waged war almost without interruption for the next 35 years. His mounted armies conquered Persia, defeated the Golden Horde in 1395, plundered Delhi in 1398 and Aleppo, Damascus, and Baghdad in 1400 and 1401, and in 1402 defeated the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I near Ankara, who died in captivity. As a warning Timur had towers built out of skulls; hundreds of thousands died in his campaigns, and whole regions were laid waste. At the same time he brought craftsmen, master builders, and scholars to Samarkand, where splendid mosques and mausoleums were built and where his grandson Ulugh Beg later erected one of the best observatories in the world. Timur died in 1405 at the start of a campaign against China; his descendant Babur founded the Mughal empire in India in 1526.

title: Jikji: the oldest surviving book printed with metal type
summary: At the Korean monastery of Heungdeoksa a collection of Buddhist teachings is printed with movable metal type, some 80 years before Gutenberg's Bible.
text: In Korea people had already experimented with movable metal type in the 13th century. The book Jikji, a selection of teachings by Buddhist Zen masters, was printed in 1377 at Heungdeoksa monastery near Cheongju. Only the second volume survives; it is now held by the National Library of France in Paris. It is regarded as the oldest surviving book produced with movable metal type. Because Chinese requires thousands of characters, however, printing in East Asia remained mainly a matter for the state and the monasteries.

title: The Peasants' Revolt in England
summary: Tens of thousands of peasants and craftsmen march on London under Wat Tyler and demand the end of serfdom.
text: After the Black Death, wage laborers had gained more bargaining power, but laws froze wages, and a poll tax for the war against France hit poor and rich equally hard. In June 1381 the counties of Kent and Essex rose up, marched on London under the leadership of Wat Tyler, opened prisons, and killed the Archbishop of Canterbury. The preacher John Ball asked where the nobleman had been when Adam delved and Eve span. The fourteen-year-old king Richard II promised the abolition of serfdom, but after Tyler was struck down during the negotiations the revolt was put down; serfdom nevertheless largely disappeared in England over the following decades.

title: Battle of Kosovo
summary: On the Field of Blackbirds in Kosovo the Ottomans fight a Serbian army; both rulers are killed, and Serbia becomes a tributary of the Ottomans.
text: On 15 June 1389 Sultan Murad I and the Serbian prince Lazar met with their armies on the Field of Blackbirds near Priština. Murad was killed during the battle by a Serbian nobleman whom tradition calls Miloš Obilić; Lazar was captured and executed. Murad's son Bayezid I took command, and Serbia soon had to pay tribute and provide troops. In Serbian memory the battle became a myth of sacrifice and loyalty that still has political effects today.

title: Founding of the Joseon dynasty in Korea
summary: General Yi Seong-gye overthrows the kingdom of Goryeo and founds the Joseon dynasty, which rules Korea for more than 500 years.
text: Towards the end of the 14th century the kingdom of Goryeo had been weakened by attacks of Japanese pirates and by disputes over relations with the Ming. In 1388 General Yi Seong-gye turned his army back instead of marching against China and in 1392 had himself proclaimed king. He moved the capital to Hanyang, present-day Seoul. The new dynasty made Neo-Confucianism the foundation of state, family and education and pushed back the influence of Buddhist monasteries. Joseon lasted until the end of the 19th century.

title: Rise of the Sultanate of Malacca
summary: On the strait between the Malay Peninsula and Sumatra, Malacca becomes the most important hub for trade between the Indian Ocean and China.
text: Around 1400 Parameswara, a prince from Palembang on Sumatra, founded the city of Malacca. He placed himself under the protection of the Ming and received Zheng He's fleets several times. Soon the rulers adopted Islam, and Malacca became a centre from which Islam spread across the Malay world. Merchants from Gujarat, Persia, China and Java exchanged spices, textiles and porcelain here; contemporaries reported dozens of languages being spoken in the streets. In 1511 the Portuguese conquered the city.

title: Battle of Ankara and the Ottoman Interregnum
summary: Timur defeats and captures Sultan Bayezid I; for a decade the Ottoman Empire falls apart in a war between brothers.
text: On 28 July 1402 Sultan Bayezid I, called "the Thunderbolt" because of his rapid campaigns, faced Timur's army near Ankara. Tatar horsemen and troops of Anatolian princes defected to Timur, and Bayezid was taken prisoner; he died in captivity in 1403. Timur reinstated the Anatolian princes whom the Ottomans had subjugated. Until 1413 Bayezid's sons fought over the succession, until Mehmed I reunited the empire. The crisis gave Byzantium half a century's reprieve.

title: The voyages of Zheng He
summary: On behalf of the Ming emperors, Admiral Zheng He leads seven huge fleets through Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean as far as Arabia and East Africa.
text: In 1405 the Yongle emperor sent out a fleet of dozens of enormous treasure ships and numerous escort vessels with almost 28,000 men under the eunuch Zheng He. On seven voyages the ships visited Java, Malacca, Ceylon, Calicut, Hormuz, the Arabian Peninsula and the coast of East Africa. They brought gifts, called for tribute missions and returned with gems, spices and even giraffes. After 1433 the court ended the costly voyages and turned to the defence of the northern frontier. The fleets show that China was then building the largest ocean-going ships in the world.

title: Building of the Forbidden City in Beijing
summary: The Yongle emperor has a vast palace complex built in Beijing and moves the Ming capital from Nanjing to the north.
text: As a prince, Yongle had resided in Beijing, and he wanted to move the capital closer to the northern frontier threatened by the Mongols. From 1406 hundreds of thousands of craftsmen and labourers worked on a palace complex with hundreds of buildings surrounded by walls and moats. The complex was finished in 1420, and in 1421 Beijing officially became the capital. It was called the Forbidden City because ordinary people were not allowed to enter it. Until 1912, 24 emperors of the Ming and Qing lived here; today it is a museum.

title: Ulugh Beg builds the Samarkand observatory
summary: Timur's grandson Ulugh Beg builds a great observatory in Samarkand whose star catalogue is among the most accurate of the pre-telescopic era.
text: Ulugh Beg governed Samarkand on behalf of his father and was more interested in mathematics and astronomy than in war. In the 1420s he had a three-storey observatory built on a hill, with a huge measuring arc set into the rock. His astronomers determined the positions of about 1,000 stars and the length of the year with great accuracy. In 1449 Ulugh Beg was murdered at the instigation of his own son. His tables were later translated and used in Europe as well.

title: The Aztec Triple Alliance
summary: Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan join forces and found the Aztec empire.
text: For a long time the Mexica of Tenochtitlan had to pay tribute to the Tepanecs of Azcapotzalco. In 1428 their ruler Itzcoatl, together with Nezahualcoyotl of Texcoco and the city of Tlacopan, defeated the Tepanecs. The three cities formed an alliance, subjugated large parts of Mexico in the following decades and shared the tribute. Over time Tenochtitlan became the leading power. Around 1500 hundreds of cities from the Gulf coast to the Pacific paid levies to the Triple Alliance.

title: Lê Lợi frees Đại Việt from Ming rule
summary: After ten years of rebellion, Lê Lợi drives the Chinese occupiers out of Vietnam and founds the Lê dynasty.
text: In 1407 the Ming had conquered the Vietnamese state of Đại Việt and tried to turn it into a Chinese province. From 1418 the landowner Lê Lợi led an uprising that began with raids from the mountains and finally defeated the Ming armies. In 1427 the Chinese withdrew, and in 1428 Lê Lợi ascended the throne as emperor. His adviser Nguyễn Trãi wrote a famous proclamation on the victory. Under the Lê dynasty Đại Việt later expanded southwards at the expense of the kingdom of Champa.

title: Rise of the Mutapa empire
summary: After the decline of Great Zimbabwe, Shona rulers establish the empire of Mutapa in the north of the plateau.
text: According to tradition, the Shona prince Nyatsimba Mutota moved around 1430 from the region of Great Zimbabwe northwards to the Zambezi and subjugated numerous groups there. His successors bore the title Mwene Mutapa and controlled the gold and ivory trade with the Swahili merchants on the coast. In the 16th century the Portuguese pushed up the Zambezi to gain access to the gold mines. In 1629 a Mutapa ruler was forced to sign a treaty that made him dependent on Portugal. Nevertheless the empire survived in reduced form into the 19th century.

title: End of Angkor as the Khmer capital
summary: After an attack from Ayutthaya, the Khmer kings abandon their old capital of Angkor and move their seat to the south.
text: From the 9th to the 13th century the Khmer empire had dominated large parts of Southeast Asia. In the 14th and 15th centuries it came under growing pressure from the kingdom of Ayutthaya, whose troops, according to tradition, captured Angkor in 1431. The kings then moved their seat to the area of present-day Phnom Penh, closer to the trade routes on the Mekong. Researchers cite the decay of the irrigation system and droughts as further causes. Angkor Wat, however, remained an important Buddhist pilgrimage site.

title: Brunelleschi completes the dome of Florence Cathedral
summary: Filippo Brunelleschi completes the huge dome of Santa Maria del Fiore, the emblem of the early Renaissance.
text: Work on the cathedral of Florence had been going on since 1296, but no one knew how the opening, more than 40 meters wide, could be vaulted over. In 1420 Brunelleschi designed a double-shelled dome that was built without wooden centering, and for it he invented hoisting machines and a herringbone pattern of brickwork. On 25 March 1436 Pope Eugene IV consecrated the cathedral; the dome remained the largest masonry dome in the world into the 20th century and proved that the builders of the present could surpass antiquity.

title: Pachacuti builds up the Inca empire
summary: An Inca ruler turns the small kingdom of Cusco into a great empire that soon stretches across the whole of the Andes.
text: Around 1438 the prince Cusi Yupanqui repelled an attack by the Chanka on Cusco, dethroned his father, and took the name Pachacuti, he who overturns the world. In a good three decades he subdued the peoples of the highlands, had Cusco laid out anew as the capital, and introduced storehouses, labor service, and administration by means of knotted cords, the quipus. The mountain city of Machu Picchu was probably built under him as well. His successors extended the empire of the four parts, Tawantinsuyu, from Ecuador to Chile; with around ten million inhabitants it was the largest empire in the Americas when the Spaniards arrived in 1532.

title: Oba Ewuare renews the kingdom of Benin
summary: Under Oba Ewuare, Benin becomes a powerful kingdom with a fortified capital and a famous court art.
text: Ewuare, known as the Great, came to power around 1440 as oba, or king, of Benin in what is now southern Nigeria. He rebuilt the capital with broad streets and a vast system of earthen walls and moats and expanded the kingdom through military campaigns. At court, guilds of casters and carvers made commemorative heads, relief plaques and ivory works for the ancestral altars of the kings. From the 1480s Benin traded with Portuguese merchants. The works known as the Benin Bronzes were looted by British troops in 1897; their return is still being negotiated today.

title: King Sejong promulgates the Hangeul script
summary: The Korean king Sejong publishes a new, easy-to-learn alphabet so that ordinary people too can read and write.
text: Until then Koreans wrote with Chinese characters, which only a small educated elite had mastered. In 1443 King Sejong had a script developed with originally 28 letters, some of whose shapes depict the position of the speech organs. In 1446 it was promulgated under the title Hunminjeongeum, the correct sounds for the instruction of the people. Many scholars rejected the script as a threat to Chinese learning. Hangeul only fully prevailed in the 20th century; today South Korea celebrates Hangeul Day every year.

title: The building of Machu Picchu
summary: High above the Urubamba Valley a royal estate of the Inca is built.
text: Machu Picchu lies on a mountain saddle at about 2,400 meters above sea level, some 450 meters above the Urubamba valley. The complex was probably built as an estate for Pachacuti; new radiocarbon dates show that it was already inhabited in the 1420s. Temples, houses and terraces are built of precisely fitted stones, and a canal supplied the inhabitants with spring water. The Spaniards never found the site. In 1911 the American Hiram Bingham made it known worldwide; since 1983 it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

title: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy
summary: Five peoples in northeastern North America unite under the Great Law of Peace.
text: According to tradition, the Peacemaker Deganawida and his companion Hiawatha ended the blood feuds between the Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga and Seneca in today's state of New York. The five peoples agreed on the Great Law of Peace and a joint council at Onondaga, which made decisions by consensus. The clan mothers chose the council members and could also remove them. When the confederacy arose is disputed; suggestions range from the 12th to the 16th century. In the 18th century the Tuscarora joined as the sixth nation.

title: Gutenberg invents printing with movable type
summary: In Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg develops a printing process using movable metal type and a printing press.
text: Gutenberg combined cast individual letters made of a lead alloy, a printing press modeled on the wine press, and an oil-based printing ink. Around 1454 he completed the forty-two-line Bible, the first great printed book of Europe. Within fifty years printing shops had been set up in more than 250 European cities, and books became affordable for many people.

title: The fall of Constantinople
summary: The Ottomans under Mehmed II capture the Byzantine capital and bring the Eastern Roman Empire to an end.
text: After almost two months of siege, Ottoman troops broke through the walls of Constantinople on 29 May 1453 with the help of enormous cannon; the last emperor, Constantine XI, fell in the fighting. Sultan Mehmed II made the city, under the name Istanbul, the capital of his empire and had the Hagia Sophia converted into a mosque. Many regard the event as the end of the Middle Ages: Greek scholars fled to Italy and fostered the Renaissance there, and the search for new trade routes to Asia accelerated the European voyages of exploration.

title: Construction of the Topkapı Palace
summary: Mehmed II has a new palace built at the tip of Istanbul's old city, which remains the seat of government of the sultans for almost 400 years.
text: A few years after the conquest of Constantinople, Mehmed II began building a new palace around 1459 on the hill above the Bosporus and the Golden Horn. The Topkapı Palace was a sequence of courtyards: in the outer area the Divan, the imperial council, met, while the inner area housed the palace school, where young pages were trained as officers and officials. The harem housed the sultan's family. Only in 1856 did the court move to the Dolmabahçe Palace; since 1924 Topkapı has been a museum.

title: Qhapaq Ñan: the road network of the Inca
summary: A road system of over 30,000 kilometers links the Inca empire from Ecuador to Chile.
text: The Inca improved older paths and linked them into a network with two main routes, one through the highlands and one along the coast. Stairways, causeways and suspension bridges of woven grass crossed gorges and swamps. At regular intervals there were way stations and storehouses, the tambos. Relay runners, the chasquis, carried messages and quipus over hundreds of kilometers in a few days. The roads served the army, the administration and labor service; since 2014 they have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site in six countries.

title: Muhammad Rumfa reforms the Hausa state of Kano
summary: The ruler of Kano develops his city into the leading center of trade and learning among the Hausa states.
text: The Hausa states in the north of present-day Nigeria were independent city-states such as Kano, Katsina and Zaria that lived from crafts, agriculture and long-distance trade. Muhammad Rumfa, who according to the Kano Chronicle ruled from about 1463 to 1499, extended the city walls, founded the great Kurmi market and had a new palace built. He brought Muslim scholars to his court, among them the North African jurist al-Maghili, who wrote a treatise for him on the obligations of princes. Kano became famous for its indigo-dyed cotton cloth and leather goods. For centuries the city remained one of the most important markets in West Africa.

title: Sunni Ali conquers Timbuktu
summary: The ruler of Songhai wrests Timbuktu from the Tuareg and makes Songhai the new great power on the Niger.
text: Songhai, with its capital Gao, had long been dependent on Mali until it turned conqueror in the 15th century under Sunni Ali. In 1468 he took Timbuktu, which had been under Tuareg control since 1433, and dealt harshly with some of its scholars.
