A few years later, after a long siege, he also conquered the trading city of Djenné. With a fleet of boats on the Niger and strong cavalry he created the largest empire West Africa had yet seen. After his death in 1492, Askia Mohammed seized power.

title: The Inca conquer the Chimú kingdom
summary: Under Tupac Yupanqui the Inca subjugate their greatest rival on the coast of Peru.
text: While his father Pachacuti was still alive, Tupac Yupanqui led the Inca armies northward. Around 1470 he subjugated the rich kingdom of Chimor on the north coast, probably in part by threatening the water supply of its valleys. The Chimú king was taken to Cusco, as were many gold- and silversmiths, whose art adorned the Inca court. With the victory over Chimor the Inca controlled the entire coast of Peru. As ruler, Tupac Yupanqui then extended the empire into Ecuador and deep into Chile.

title: The king of Kongo is baptized
summary: King Nzinga a Nkuwu receives baptism in his capital and seeks an alliance with Portugal.
text: In 1483 the Portuguese navigator Diogo Cão had reached the mouth of the Congo River and made contact with the kingdom of Kongo, a large, well-organized state in present-day Angola and Congo. Envoys travelled to Lisbon, and in 1491 priests, craftsmen and soldiers arrived in the capital Mbanza Kongo. King Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptized there and took the name João I. He hoped the alliance would bring him prestige, weapons and knowledge. Later he partly turned away from Christianity again, but his son Afonso made it the state religion.

title: The fall of Granada
summary: The last emir of Granada hands the city over to Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon; Muslim rule in Spain ends after almost 800 years.
text: From 1482 the Catholic Monarchs Isabella and Ferdinand waged war against the Emirate of Granada, weakened by family strife, and took city after city. After a siege lasting months, Emir Muhammad XII, whom the Spaniards called Boabdil, handed over the Alhambra on 2 January 1492; according to legend he wept at his last sight of the city. The treaty of surrender guaranteed the Muslims freedom of religion and their property, yet as early as around 1500 they were forced to be baptized, and from 1609 to 1614 Spain expelled the descendants of these Moriscos. In that same year, 1492, the Jews had to leave Spain, and Columbus sailed west on the monarchs' commission. With Granada the Reconquista came to an end, the reconquest of the peninsula by the Christian kingdoms, which had begun in 711 with the Arab conquest.

title: Columbus reaches America
summary: In search of a sea route to India, Christopher Columbus lands on an island in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492.
text: With three ships Columbus had sailed west from Palos on the commission of the Spanish crown, because he believed the earth to be smaller than it is. Until his death he believed that he had reached the east coast of Asia. In fact his landing began the lasting contact between Europe and America, which fundamentally changed the history of both continents.

title: Askia Mohammed takes power in the Songhai empire
summary: With Askia Mohammed begins the golden age of the Songhai empire, the largest state in West Africa, with Timbuktu as a center of scholarship.
text: After the death of the conqueror Sunni Ali, the general Mohammed Ture overthrew his son and took the ruler's title of Askia. He reorganized the empire on the Niger with provinces, officials, and a professional army, made the pilgrimage to Mecca in 1496, and promoted Islam as a unifying religion. Timbuktu with its Sankoré Mosque, and Djenné, became centers of Islamic scholarship whose manuscripts survive to this day. Trade in gold, salt, and slaves across the Sahara made Songhai one of the richest powers of the age; in 1591 it was shattered by Moroccan troops with firearms.

title: Treaty of Tordesillas
summary: Spain and Portugal divide the newly discovered lands of the world, and those still to be discovered, between them along a line in the Atlantic.
text: After the return of Columbus, the two sea powers quarreled over the rights to the new lands, and in 1493 Pope Alexander VI proposed a dividing line. In the treaty of 7 June 1494 it was fixed 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands: everything west of it was to belong to Spain, everything east of it to Portugal. Brazil, reached in 1500, thus fell to Portugal, which is still evident today in the language of the country. Other powers such as England and France never recognized the division; the treaty shows how matter-of-factly European rulers disposed of foreign continents.

title: Vasco da Gama reaches India
summary: The Portuguese Vasco da Gama sails around Africa and is the first European to reach India by sea.
text: After a voyage of almost a year around the Cape of Good Hope, da Gama landed at Calicut on the Malabar Coast of India in May 1498. The new sea route bypassed the Arab and Venetian middlemen and made Portugal the leading power in the spice trade for a century. Portuguese bases were soon established from East Africa as far as China and Japan.

title: Pedro Álvares Cabral reaches Brazil
summary: A Portuguese fleet on its way to India lands on the coast of Brazil and takes possession of the land for Portugal.
text: Pedro Álvares Cabral was to follow Vasco da Gama's route to India with thirteen ships, but sailed far out to the west into the Atlantic. On 22 April 1500 the fleet sighted land on the coast of today's state of Bahia. Cabral had a cross erected and claimed the territory, which under the Treaty of Tordesillas lay east of the dividing line, for the Portuguese Crown. The scribe Pero Vaz de Caminha described the first encounter with the Tupí in a letter to the king. At first Brazil was used mainly for its red brazilwood, which gave the country its name.

title: Ismail I founds the Safavid Empire
summary: The young leader of a Sufi order captures Tabriz, has himself crowned shah and makes Twelver Shiism the state religion of Persia.
text: The Safavids were originally the heads of a Sufi order in Ardabil whose followers were mainly Turkmen warriors with red caps, the Qizilbash. In 1501 the roughly fourteen-year-old Ismail captured Tabriz and had himself proclaimed shah. Within a few years he subjugated all of Iran and declared the Twelver branch of Shiism the state religion, which he enforced even against the resistance of the Sunni majority. In 1514 he was defeated by the Ottomans at Chaldiran. The Safavids laid the foundations of modern Iran.

title: Michelangelo completes the David
summary: Michelangelo's marble statue of David, more than five meters high, is set up in Florence.
text: Michelangelo Buonarroti created the figure from a block of marble on which other sculptors had previously tried their hand in vain. The statue shows the biblical hero in tense stillness before the fight and became a symbol of the free republic of Florence. It is regarded as a masterpiece of the High Renaissance, which depicted the human body in perfect form after the model of antiquity.

title: Montesinos' sermon and the Laws of Burgos
summary: After sharp criticism from Dominican friars, the Spanish Crown issues the first regulations to protect Indigenous people in the encomienda.
text: On Hispaniola Spanish settlers had been allotted Indigenous people under the encomienda system and forced them to work in gold mines and fields. In Advent 1511 the Dominican Antonio de Montesinos accused the settlers in a sermon of mortal sin and asked whether the Indigenous people were not human beings. In response King Ferdinand issued the Laws of Burgos in December 1512, which regulated working hours, food and religious instruction. They did not call the encomienda itself into question, and in practice they were hardly obeyed.

title: Battle of Chaldiran
summary: Selim I defeats the Persian shah Ismail I and secures eastern Anatolia for the Ottomans.
text: The Safavid shah Ismail I had made Shiite Islam the state religion of Persia and found followers among the Turkmen tribes of Anatolia. Sultan Selim I had these followers persecuted and marched against Persia in 1514. On 23 August 1514 he won at Chaldiran in what is now northwestern Iran, above all thanks to his artillery and the Janissaries armed with firearms. Selim briefly occupied Tabriz, and eastern Anatolia came under Ottoman rule. The border between the Sunni Ottoman Empire and Shiite Persia shaped the region for centuries.

title: Erasmus publishes the Greek New Testament
summary: The first printed edition of the New Testament in Greek, a key work of humanism, appears in Basel.
text: For his Novum Instrumentum, Erasmus of Rotterdam compared several manuscripts, set the original Greek text alongside a Latin translation of his own, and added critical notes. In doing so he called into question the Latin Vulgate, authoritative for centuries, and demanded that every Christian should read the Bible for himself. Luther used the second edition of 1519 for his German translation of the New Testament, and Tyndale and Calvin also built on it. Printing made the work available throughout Europe within a few years.

title: Luther publishes the 95 Theses
summary: The Wittenberg theologian Martin Luther criticizes the trade in indulgences in 95 theses and sets off the Reformation.
text: Luther opposed the idea that one could buy release from the punishment for sins by purchasing letters of indulgence. Thanks to printing, his theses spread across the whole of Germany within a few weeks. In 1521 he refused to recant at the Diet of Worms, was outlawed, and at the Wartburg translated the New Testament into German.

title: Selim I conquers Egypt
summary: With the victory over the Mamluks the Ottomans gain Syria, Egypt and the protectorate over Mecca and Medina.
text: In August 1516 Selim I defeated the Mamluk army at Marj Dabiq north of Aleppo; their sultan al-Ghawri was killed. In January 1517 the Ottomans beat the last Mamluk force at Ridaniya outside Cairo and had the Mamluk sultan Tuman Bay executed. The sharif of Mecca submitted, and Selim called himself Servant of the Two Holy Sanctuaries. He took the last Abbasid shadow caliph to Istanbul; later sultans derived their claim to the caliphate from this. The empire became the leading power of the Arab world.

title: The first circumnavigation of the world under Magellan
summary: A Spanish fleet under Ferdinand Magellan sails around the earth for the first time and proves in practice that it is a sphere.
text: In the south of America Magellan found the strait named after him and crossed the Pacific, which he so named because of its calm sea. He himself died in 1521 in the Philippines in a fight with local people. Only one ship, the Victoria under Juan Sebastián Elcano, returned to Spain in 1522 with 18 survivors.

title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
summary: Spanish conquistadors under Hernán Cortés capture the capital of the Aztecs.
text: Cortés had landed in Mexico in 1519 with a few hundred soldiers and had allied himself with peoples who suffered under Aztec rule. After a siege lasting months, in which smallpox and hunger weakened the defenders, Tenochtitlan fell in August 1521. On the ruins of the city arose Mexico City, the capital of the Spanish viceroyalty of New Spain.

title: Diet of Worms: Luther refuses to recant
summary: Before Emperor Charles V, Martin Luther refuses to recant his teachings and is thereupon placed under the imperial ban.
text: After the pope had excommunicated Luther, the young emperor summoned him to Worms with a guarantee of safe conduct. On 18 April 1521 Luther declared before the emperor and the imperial estates that he could recant only if he were refuted from Holy Scripture, for to act against conscience was neither safe nor wholesome. The Edict of Worms declared him a heretic and banned his writings, but the elector Frederick the Wise had him abducted for appearance's sake and hidden at the Wartburg. There Luther translated the New Testament into German in just eleven weeks.

title: The German Peasants' War
summary: Peasants in southern and central Germany rise up against dues and serfdom and are bloodily put down.
text: Encouraged by the Reformation, the peasants demanded in the Twelve Articles of Memmingen the free election of pastors, the end of serfdom, and lower dues. Luther sharply condemned the revolt and took the side of the princes. The armies of the Swabian League defeated the peasants at Frankenhausen among other places; around 70,000 people lost their lives.

title: Afonso I of Kongo protests against the slave trade
summary: In letters to the king of Portugal, the Christian king of Kongo complains that traders are carrying off free subjects.
text: Afonso I ruled Kongo from 1509 as a committed Christian, had churches and schools built and sent young nobles to Portugal to be educated. At the same time the trade in captives grew, whom Portuguese merchants took to São Tomé and soon to Brazil. In 1526 Afonso wrote to King João III that traders were seizing and selling even free people and members of the nobility, thereby depopulating the country. He demanded that the trade be placed under royal supervision and asked for priests and teachers instead of merchants. His letters are among the earliest African testimonies to the consequences of the Atlantic slave trade.

title: The beginning of the transatlantic slave trade
summary: For the first time, enslaved Africans are carried off directly from the West African coast to America.
text: Because the indigenous population of America was dying in great numbers from disease and violence, the colonial rulers looked for labor for plantations and mines. Portuguese and later Spanish, English, French, and Dutch traders bought or seized people on the African coast and carried them across the Atlantic under cruel conditions. By the 19th century more than twelve million people had been carried off in this way.

title: First Battle of Panipat: Babur founds the Mughal Empire
summary: With field guns and muskets, Babur defeats the far larger army of the Sultan of Delhi and founds the Mughal Empire.
text: Babur, a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, had lost his homeland in the Fergana Valley and launched several advances into India from Kabul. On 21 April 1526 he met the army of Ibrahim Lodi, the last Sultan of Delhi, at Panipat north of Delhi. Babur combined a wagon fortress, field artillery and muskets with flanking attacks by his cavalry and won; Ibrahim was killed. In 1527 he also defeated the Rajput princes. His successors, the Great Mughals, ruled India for more than 300 years.

title: Battle of Mohács
summary: Suleiman the Magnificent destroys the Hungarian army; King Louis II is killed, and the Kingdom of Hungary falls apart.
text: On 29 August 1526 Suleiman's troops met the much smaller army of King Louis II of Hungary and Bohemia at Mohács on the Danube. The Ottoman artillery and the Janissaries decided the battle within a few hours; Louis drowned while fleeing. The Habsburg Ferdinand and the Hungarian nobleman John Zápolya disputed his succession. In 1541 the Ottomans took Buda, and central Hungary became an Ottoman province for 150 years. Hungary remained divided between the Habsburgs, the Ottomans and the Principality of Transylvania.

title: Death of Huayna Capac and the war of the brothers
summary: An epidemic kills the Inca Huayna Capac, and his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa fight for power.
text: Around 1527 Huayna Capac died in the north of the empire of an epidemic, probably smallpox, which spread from the European settlements faster than the Spaniards themselves. His designated successor also died. Thereupon two sons claimed the throne: Huáscar, who was recognized in Cusco, and Atahualpa, who relied on the experienced army in the north. The civil war devastated wide areas. In 1532 Atahualpa's generals captured Huáscar, shortly before Francisco Pizarro and his men arrived in the empire.

title: Ethiopia at war with Ahmad Gragn
summary: The imam of the Sultanate of Adal conquers large parts of Christian Ethiopia until he is defeated with Portuguese help.
text: Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim, called Gragn, the left-handed, by the Ethiopians, led the troops of the Muslim Sultanate of Adal in the east of the Horn of Africa. After his victory at Shimbra Kure in 1529 he overran large parts of the empire with firearms obtained from the Ottoman Empire and destroyed many churches and monasteries. Emperor Lebna Dengel died in 1540 while in flight. His son Galawdewos received support from a small Portuguese force and defeated Ahmad in 1543 at Wayna Daga, where the imam was killed. The war weakened both sides and made it easier for the Oromo to migrate into the highlands.

title: First siege of Vienna
summary: Suleiman besieges the Habsburg residence of Vienna, but has to withdraw after three weeks.
text: After taking Buda and installing John Zápolya as vassal king, Suleiman advanced up the Danube with a large army in 1529 and encircled Vienna at the end of September. The city was defended by a small garrison under Count Niklas Salm, which repelled several mines and assaults. Long supply lines, rain and the approaching winter forced the Ottomans to withdraw in mid-October. The siege shocked Europe and, in the Holy Roman Empire, intensified the fear of the "Turks" spread by pamphlets and sermons. In the following years the Turkish threat repeatedly obliged Emperor Charles V to make concessions to the Protestants, whose help he needed.

title: The conquest of the Inca empire
summary: Francisco Pizarro takes the Inca ruler Atahualpa prisoner and brings the largest empire in South America under Spanish control.
text: With fewer than 200 men, Pizarro lured the Inca Atahualpa into an ambush at Cajamarca and had his retinue slaughtered. Despite an enormous ransom in gold and silver, Atahualpa was executed in 1533. A preceding civil war and imported epidemics had weakened the empire; in 1535 the Spaniards founded Lima and exploited the silver mines of Potosí.

title: Founding of the Viceroyalty of New Spain
summary: With Antonio de Mendoza the first viceroy takes office in Mexico City; the Crown takes over rule from the conquistadors.
text: After the conquest of the Aztec Empire, Emperor Charles V distrusted the power of the conquistadors and installed a direct representative. In 1535 Antonio de Mendoza arrived in Mexico City as the first viceroy and built up the administration, the tax system and a mint. New Spain eventually stretched from the territory of today's United States through Central America and the Caribbean to the Philippines. In 1542 the Viceroyalty of Peru followed, with its capital Lima. The viceroyalties lasted for almost three centuries until independence.

title: The New Laws ban the enslavement of Indigenous people
summary: Charles V declares Indigenous people free subjects of the Crown and intends to let the encomienda expire.
text: Under the impact of the reports of Bartolomé de Las Casas, Charles V signed the New Laws in November 1542. They banned the enslavement of Indigenous people, prohibited the granting of new encomiendas and decreed that existing ones should revert to the Crown on the death of their holders. In Peru settlers under Gonzalo Pizarro rose up in response and killed the viceroy in 1546. The Crown withdrew the inheritance rule in 1545, yet the encomienda gradually lost importance. The laws are regarded as early evidence of a debate about human rights.

title: Copernicus publishes the heliocentric model of the universe
summary: In his principal work, Nicolaus Copernicus places the sun rather than the earth at the center of the universe.
text: The book De revolutionibus orbium coelestium appeared in Nuremberg shortly before the death of its author. Copernicus explained the movements of the planets more simply by having the earth circle the sun, and in doing so he contradicted the teaching of Ptolemy, which had been accepted since antiquity. His model was later confirmed and developed further by Kepler, Galileo, and Newton, and it marks the beginning of modern astronomy.

title: Vesalius founds modern anatomy
summary: With his work De humani corporis fabrica, Andreas Vesalius replaces the ancient teaching of Galen with observations of the dissected human body.
text: Vesalius, who came from Brussels, taught in Padua and dissected himself instead of watching an assistant and reading aloud from Galen, as was usual. In doing so he found more than 200 errors in ancient anatomy, which Galen had derived from animals. His work in seven books, printed in Basel in 1543, combined precise descriptions with masterly woodcuts from the workshop of Titian. The Fabrica made the human body an object of independent research and became the foundation of scientific medicine.

title: Discovery of the silver mountain of Potosí
summary: In the highlands of today's Bolivia the Spaniards come upon the Cerro Rico, the richest silver deposit of the early modern period.
text: At the foot of the Cerro Rico, at an altitude of more than 4,000 metres, one of the largest cities in the Americas grew up within a few decades. From the 1570s Viceroy Francisco de Toledo obliged Indigenous villages under the mita system to send thousands of men to the mines every year. With the amalgamation process and mercury from Huancavelica, output rose sharply, but many workers died from accidents, cold and poisoning. Silver from Potosí financed Spain's wars and travelled via Europe as far as China. To this day the name Potosí stands for both immeasurable wealth and exploitation.

title: Council of Trent
summary: The Catholic Church responds to the Reformation with a clarification of its teaching and with internal reforms.
text: In three sessions over 18 years, the bishops affirmed the Catholic doctrine of the sacraments, of tradition, and of justification, and marked it off clearly from the Protestant positions. At the same time abuses such as the sale of offices were combated and seminaries were established for better training. The council shaped Catholicism into the 20th century and deepened the division of Christendom.

title: Founding of Salvador da Bahia
summary: Portugal installs a governor-general in Brazil and founds Salvador as the capital of the colony.
text: The system of private captaincies, to which Portugal had granted the Brazilian coast since 1534, had largely failed. In 1549 Tomé de Sousa arrived as the first governor-general in the Bay of All Saints and founded Salvador. With him came the first Jesuits under Manuel da Nóbrega, who began the mission among the Tupí. In the following decades sugar plantations grew in Bahia and Pernambuco, on which more and more enslaved Africans were forced to work. Salvador remained the capital of Brazil until 1763.

title: Expansion of the Great Wall under the Ming
summary: After Mongol raids reach the gates of Beijing, the Ming turn the frontier fortifications into the wall of stone and brick known today as the Great Wall.
text: The Ming emperors increasingly relied on defence against the Mongols. After the Mongol ruler Altan Khan had advanced to the outskirts of Beijing in 1550, the northern fortifications were strengthened at great expense. Especially under General Qi Jiguang, sections of brick and stone with closely spaced watchtowers were built from the late 1560s onwards. The Ming wall runs from the Shanhaiguan pass on the sea to Jiayuguan in the west. Most of the sections visited today, such as Badaling, date from this period.

title: The Valladolid debate
summary: Before a commission of scholars, Bartolomé de Las Casas and Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argue over the legitimacy of the conquest of the Americas.
text: Charles V temporarily suspended new campaigns of conquest until theologians and jurists had clarified whether war against the Indigenous peoples was permissible. Sepúlveda appealed to Aristotle and claimed that the Indigenous peoples were by nature destined for subordination. Las Casas countered that they were rational human beings with kingdoms of their own and could be led to the faith only by peaceful means. The commission reached no clear verdict. The debate is nevertheless regarded as one of Europe's first great disputes about the rights of foreign peoples.

title: Sinan builds the Süleymaniye Mosque
summary: The court architect Sinan erects for Suleiman, on one of Istanbul's hills, one of the largest mosque complexes in the Islamic world.
text: From 1550 to 1557 Sinan built the Süleymaniye Mosque on Suleiman's commission; its dome still dominates the skyline of Istanbul. The complex included madrasas, a medical school, a hospital, a soup kitchen, a caravanserai, a bath and a library. Sinan took the Hagia Sophia as his model but made the interior brighter and more clearly structured. In the garden lie the tombs of Suleiman and his wife Hürrem. The foundation shows how mosques were at the same time social and educational centres.

title: First universities in Lima and Mexico
summary: The Spanish Crown founds the first universities on the American mainland in Lima and Mexico City.
text: In May 1551 the university that survives today as the National University of San Marcos was founded in Lima, and in September a royal decree followed for the University of Mexico. On the model of Salamanca they taught theology, canon law, law, medicine and the arts. In Mexico there were also chairs for Indigenous languages such as Nahuatl, because priests were to be trained for the mission. The universities mainly educated clergy and lawyers from Creole families, who later formed the backbone of the administration.

title: Peace of Augsburg
summary: The Diet of Augsburg recognizes the Lutheran confession in the empire and leaves the choice of denomination to the territorial rulers.
text: After the Schmalkaldic War and the revolt of the princes, Charles V had come to see that the Protestants could not be forced back into the old church, and he left the negotiations to his brother Ferdinand. The peace proclaimed on 25 September 1555 granted each imperial estate the right to determine the Catholic or the Lutheran confession for its own territory; subjects of another faith were allowed to emigrate. Later this principle was summed up in the formula that whoever rules the land determines its religion. Calvinists remained excluded, and unresolved disputes contributed to the outbreak of the Thirty Years' War in 1618.

title: The first coffeehouses in Istanbul
summary: Two merchants from Syria open coffeehouses in Istanbul, which quickly become popular meeting places.
text: Coffee came from Yemen and in the 15th century was popular among Sufis, who used it to stay awake during nightly devotions. According to the Ottoman chronicler Peçevi, two men from Aleppo and Damascus opened the first coffeehouses around 1555 in Istanbul's Tahtakale quarter. There men met to talk, to play board games and to listen to poets and storytellers. Religious scholars and sultans distrusted these places of criticism; Murad IV had them closed in 1633. In the 17th century coffee reached Europe by way of Venice and Vienna.

title: Akbar becomes ruler of the Mughal empire
summary: The thirteen-year-old Akbar ascends the throne and builds the Mughal empire into the dominant power in India with a policy of religious tolerance.
text: The Mughal empire had been founded by Babur in 1526, but it was Akbar who secured it for good: after his victory at the second battle of Panipat in 1556, he subdued northern India, Gujarat, and Bengal over the following decades. He bound the Hindu Rajputs to himself through marriages and offices, abolished the special tax on non-Muslims in 1564, and had Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Parsis, and Jesuits debate with one another at his court. His administration, with a land survey for taxation and a ranking order of officials, and the buildings of Fatehpur Sikri, shaped India into the British period.

title: Oda Nobunaga wins at Okehazama and begins the unification of Japan
summary: With a surprise victory over a far superior army, the provincial lord Oda Nobunaga rises to become the leading power in a fragmented Japan.
text: Since the Ōnin War of 1467, Japan had been in the Sengoku period, the age of the warring states, broken up into dozens of principalities, while the shogun in Kyoto was powerless. In 1560 Nobunaga attacked the camp of the lord Imagawa Yoshimoto at Okehazama with a few thousand warriors and killed him. In the following years he took Kyoto, in 1575 at Nagashino deployed muskets in great numbers, which Portuguese traders had brought into the country, and broke the power of the Buddhist monasteries. After his death in 1582, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu completed the unification of the country.

title: Silver fleets and the Manila galleon
summary: Andrés de Urdaneta finds the return route across the Pacific; Spanish fleets now link the Americas with Europe and Asia.
text: To protect itself against pirates and hostile powers, Spain had its ships sail in armed convoys from the middle of the 16th century: every year one fleet sailed to Veracruz and one to Cartagena and Panama, and together they brought silver to Seville. In 1565 the navigator and friar Andrés de Urdaneta discovered a route that led back from the Philippines to Mexico with favourable winds. From then on the Manila galleon linked Acapulco with Manila, where Mexican silver was exchanged for Chinese silk and porcelain. For the first time a trade network arose that spanned all inhabited continents. The galleon sailed until 1815.

title: Idris Alooma makes Bornu a military power
summary: The king of Bornu strengthens his realm with firearms, Turkish instructors and Islamic law.
text: Idris Alooma ruled Kanem-Bornu in the late 16th century; the exact years of his reign are disputed among historians. He obtained muskets and instructors from Ottoman-ruled Tripoli and with them raised a corps of musketeers that gave him military superiority over his neighbors. In numerous campaigns he extended his rule around Lake Chad and also regained the old heartland of Kanem. After a pilgrimage to Mecca he promoted Islamic law, mosques and scholars. His court chronicler Ahmad ibn Furtu described his deeds in detail.

title: Naval battle of Lepanto
summary: The fleet of the Holy League under Don John of Austria defeats the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras.
text: After the Ottomans had attacked Venetian Cyprus in 1570, Spain, Venice and the pope formed the Holy League. On 7 October 1571 more than 400 warships met in the Gulf of Patras; the League's fleet under Don John of Austria won, and the Ottoman admiral Ali Pasha was killed. Among the wounded was the future writer Miguel de Cervantes. Europe celebrated the victory, but the Ottomans rebuilt their fleet within a year and kept Cyprus, which Venice ceded in 1573.

title: St. Bartholomew's Day massacre in Paris
summary: In the night of 24 August 1572, thousands of Huguenots are murdered in Paris; the massacre becomes a symbol of the wars of religion.
text: Numerous Huguenot leaders had come to Paris for the wedding of the Protestant Henry of Navarre to Marguerite de Valois, the king's sister. After a failed attempt on the life of Admiral Coligny, the court, under the influence of the queen mother Catherine de' Medici, had the leaders killed; the mob widened the violence into a massacre that claimed up to 10,000 victims in Paris and the provinces. The pope had a commemorative medal struck; Protestant princes were appalled. The wars of religion ended only in 1598, when Henry IV, by then a Catholic, granted the Huguenots freedom of worship with the Edict of Nantes.

title: Introduction of the Gregorian calendar
summary: Pope Gregory XIII reforms the calendar: 4 October 1582 is followed immediately by 15 October.
text: The Julian calendar, in force since Caesar, had fallen ten days behind the solar year, so that Easter moved further and further away from the beginning of spring. A commission around the astronomer Christopher Clavius calculated a new rule for leap years, according to which full centuries are leap years only if they are divisible by 400. Catholic countries adopted the reform at once, the Protestant territories of Germany only in 1700, Great Britain in 1752, and Russia in 1918. Today the Gregorian calendar is the basis of the civil year worldwide.

title: Yermak begins the conquest of Siberia
summary: The Cossack leader Yermak captures the capital of the Khanate of Sibir and opens Russia's way across northern Asia to the Pacific.
text: The Stroganov merchant family recruited Cossacks under their leader Yermak to protect their estates in the Urals. In 1582 Yermak crossed the mountains with a few hundred men and captured Qashliq, the capital of Khan Kuchum. Yermak was killed in 1585, but the tsar sent more troops and had fortresses such as Tobolsk built. Lured by the valuable fur of the sable, Cossacks and traders moved east along the rivers and reached the Pacific in 1639. The indigenous peoples had to pay tribute in furs.

title: The defeat of the Spanish Armada
summary: Philip II's invasion fleet fails in the English Channel against the English fleet and against storms; England holds its own as a Protestant sea power.
text: With around 130 ships Philip II intended to ferry an army from the Netherlands to England in order to overthrow Elizabeth I and restore Catholicism. The more maneuverable English ships under Howard and Drake fired on the Armada from a distance, fireships broke up its formation off Calais, and at Gravelines it suffered heavy losses. On the way home around Scotland and Ireland, storms destroyed a large part of the fleet; only about two thirds of the ships returned. The victory consolidated Elizabeth's rule, strengthened English self-confidence, and set in motion England's rise as a sea power.

title: Battle of Tondibi and the end of the Songhai Empire
summary: A Moroccan army with firearms crosses the Sahara and defeats the army of Songhai.
text: The Moroccan sultan Ahmad al-Mansur wanted to bring the gold sources of West Africa under his control. He sent an army of a few thousand men under the Spanish-born commander Judar Pasha across the Sahara. At Tondibi near Gao, in March 1591, the troops, armed with muskets and cannon, met the far larger army of Askia Ishaq II and defeated it. Songhai fell apart, Timbuktu and Gao came under Moroccan rule, and leading scholars were deported to Marrakesh. The hoped-for quantities of gold never reached Morocco, however, and the region broke up into smaller lordships.

title: The Imjin War: Japan's invasion of Korea
summary: Toyotomi Hideyoshi has Korea attacked in order to conquer China but fails against Korean resistance, Yi Sun-sin's fleet and Ming troops.
text: After unifying Japan, Hideyoshi planned the conquest of China and demanded free passage from Korea. In 1592 more than 150,000 men landed at Busan and within a few weeks took Seoul and Pyongyang. Admiral Yi Sun-sin, however, cut the invaders' supply lines with his ships, including armoured turtle ships, and a Ming army came to Korea's aid. A second attack in 1597 also stalled. After Hideyoshi's death in 1598 the Japanese withdrew; Korea was badly devastated.

title: Abbas I makes Isfahan his capital
summary: Shah Abbas I moves the Safavid capital to Isfahan and has it developed into one of the most splendid cities in the world.
text: Abbas I had strengthened an empire hard pressed by the Ottomans and Uzbeks through reforms, and in 1598 he made Isfahan the seat of government. Around the vast Naqsh-e Jahan square rose the Ali Qapu palace, the Shah Mosque and the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque with their domes of blue tiles. Gardens, bridges and a covered bazaar made the city famous; a Persian saying called Isfahan half the world. Armenian merchants, whom Abbas settled in the suburb of New Julfa, managed the lucrative silk trade.

title: Battle of Sekigahara
summary: Tokugawa Ieyasu defeats the coalition of his rivals and lays the foundation for the Tokugawa shogunate, which rules Japan until 1868.
text: After the death of Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1598 the most powerful lords of Japan fought for supremacy. In October 1600 the Eastern Army under Tokugawa Ieyasu and the Western Army under Ishida Mitsunari clashed at Sekigahara. When several lords changed sides during the battle, Ieyasu won. In 1603 the emperor appointed him shogun, and Edo became the centre of power. With the capture of Osaka Castle in 1615 Ieyasu eliminated the last supporters of the Toyotomi.

title: The quilombo of Palmares
summary: In north-eastern Brazil the largest community of escaped enslaved people holds out for almost a century.
text: From the beginning of the 17th century enslaved people fled from the sugar plantations of Pernambuco into the forested hills of the Serra da Barriga. There Palmares arose, a federation of villages in which, according to estimates, several thousand people lived from farming, hunting and trade. The inhabitants repelled numerous attacks by Dutch and Portuguese troops. The leader Zumbi rejected a peace offer of 1678 because it left slavery outside Palmares untouched. In 1694 an army under Domingos Jorge Velho captured the main settlement, and Zumbi was killed the following year.

title: Beginning of the Jesuit reductions in Paraguay
summary: Jesuits found the first mission villages for the Guaraní on the Paraná, which soon form a large network.
text: In the reductions the Guaraní lived in planned villages with a church, workshops and jointly farmed fields under the direction of a few Jesuit fathers. The inhabitants were protected from the encomienda but had to follow Christian rules of life. Against slave raiders from São Paulo, the bandeirantes, the villages were allowed to defend themselves with militias of their own. At their peak in the 18th century well over a hundred thousand people lived in some thirty reductions. Music, wood carving and a written form of Guaraní flourished there.

title: The Thirty Years' War
summary: A war of religion and power devastates the Holy Roman Empire and draws in almost all the European powers.
text: The war began with the Defenestration of Prague, when Protestant Bohemian nobles threw imperial governors out of a window. After victories by the emperor, Denmark, Sweden under Gustavus Adolphus, and finally Catholic France intervened on the Protestant side. Mercenary armies, hunger, and epidemics killed more than a third of the population in some regions of Germany.

title: Njinga negotiates with the Portuguese in Luanda
summary: As her brother's envoy, Njinga negotiates with the Portuguese governor of Angola for peace for the kingdom of Ndongo.
text: The kingdom of Ndongo in what is now Angola suffered from the campaigns of the Portuguese, who hunted captives for the slave trade from Luanda. In 1622 Njinga, the king's sister, travelled to Luanda and negotiated a peace treaty. According to a well-known tradition, when she was offered no chair she sat on the back of a servant so as to meet the governor as an equal. She was baptized, but the Portuguese did not keep the treaty. From 1624 Njinga ruled herself and for decades waged war and diplomacy against the colonial power.

title: Kösem Sultan leads the regency
summary: When her son Murad IV becomes sultan as a child, the sultan's mother Kösem effectively governs the empire.
text: In September 1623 the eleven-year-old Murad IV was placed on the throne, and his mother Kösem conducted the business of government as valide sultan. She negotiated with viziers and Janissaries and secured the throne in a time of revolts and war with Persia. Only around 1632 did Murad take power himself. After his death in 1640 Kösem governed again for her son Ibrahim and from 1648 for her grandson Mehmed IV. Historians call this period of great influence of the palace women the "Sultanate of Women".

title: The height of the witch hunts
summary: In the years around 1630 the witch trials in central Europe reach their peak, with thousands of executions.
text: Between about 1560 and 1630, tens of thousands of people in Europe were accused as witches, forced under torture to confess, and burned; most of the victims were women, and many trials took place in the prince-bishoprics of Würzburg, Bamberg, and Cologne. The hardship of war, crop failures, and the expectation that the devil worked harm with the help of witches fueled the persecution. In 1631 the Jesuit Friedrich Spee criticized torture in the Cautio Criminalis as a source of false confessions. The trials ended only in the 18th century; the last execution in Europe took place in Switzerland in 1782.

title: Building of the Taj Mahal
summary: The Great Mughal Shah Jahan has a tomb of white marble built in Agra for his late wife Mumtaz Mahal.
text: Mumtaz Mahal, Shah Jahan's favourite wife, died in 1631 giving birth to her fourteenth child. The following year work began on the banks of the Yamuna in Agra on a mausoleum built by thousands of craftsmen from India, Persia and Central Asia. The white marble was inlaid with semi-precious stones and decorated with Quranic verses in calligraphy. The gardens, mosque and guest house were completed around 1653. The Taj Mahal is regarded as the high point of Mughal architecture and is now a World Heritage Site.

title: The trial of Galileo Galilei
summary: The Roman Inquisition condemns Galileo for his defense of the heliocentric model and forces him to recant.
text: In his Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems of 1632, Galileo had presented the teaching of Copernicus so convincingly that the church saw in it a violation of the prohibition of 1616. On 22 June 1633, almost seventy years old, he had to abjure on his knees in Rome and was sentenced to lifelong house arrest. In his villa near Florence he nevertheless wrote the Discorsi on mechanics and the laws of falling bodies, which appeared in the Netherlands in 1638. The trial became a symbol of the conflict between science and the authority of faith; the church rehabilitated Galileo only in 1992.

title: The closing of Japan under the Tokugawa
summary: The Tokugawa shogunate bars the Portuguese from entering, forbids Japanese to leave the country, and allows only the Dutch and the Chinese limited trade, which is soon confined entirely to Nagasaki.
text: Tokugawa Ieyasu had founded the shogunate in 1603 and pacified Japan after a century of civil war. His successors feared that Christian missionaries and European traders might undermine the established order, especially since a revolt of Christian peasants at Shimabara had to be bloodily put down in 1637. Through a series of decrees between 1633 and 1639, Christianity was banned, the building of ocean-going ships was forbidden, and the Portuguese were expelled; in 1641 the Dutch were moved to the artificial island of Dejima off Nagasaki. This policy, known as sakoku, lasted until 1854 and gave Japan more than two centuries of peace and a culture of its own.

title: The travels of Evliya Çelebi
summary: Evliya Çelebi of Istanbul travels through the Ottoman Empire and its neighbours for four decades and describes them in ten volumes.
text: In 1640 Evliya Çelebi began by describing Istanbul and then Bursa, and afterwards set out on journeys that until 1682 took him from Bosnia to the Caucasus, to Vienna, Mecca, Cairo and the Sudan. He often accompanied embassies and governors and wrote about cities, buildings, languages, foods, customs and crafts. His "Book of Travels" (Seyahatname) mixes precise observation with anecdotes and exaggerations. It is one of the most important sources for everyday life in the 17th century.

title: The English Civil War and the execution of Charles I
summary: In the struggle between king and parliament the parliamentary army wins; in 1649 Charles I becomes the first European monarch to be executed in public.
text: Charles I had ruled for eleven years without parliament and had tried to force an episcopal church on Scotland, until lack of money compelled him to summon parliament in 1640. The dispute over taxes, religion, and command of the army escalated into civil war in 1642 between royalists and parliamentary troops, in which Oliver Cromwell's New Model Army forced the decision at Naseby in 1645. A parliament purged by the army condemned the king for high treason, and on 30 January 1649 he was beheaded in front of his palace in London. England became a republic, and from 1653 a protectorate under Cromwell; in 1660 the monarchy returned under Charles II.

title: The Manchus take Beijing: the beginning of the Qing dynasty
summary: After rebels overthrow the Ming, the Manchus enter Beijing and found the Qing dynasty, the last imperial dynasty of China.
text: Famines, empty treasuries and peasant uprisings had weakened the Ming. In April 1644 the rebel leader Li Zicheng took Beijing, and the last Ming emperor hanged himself. The Ming general Wu Sangui then opened the Shanhaiguan pass to the Manchus, who drove out Li Zicheng and took the throne themselves. The Manchus forced Chinese men to adopt their hairstyle with a shaved forehead and a queue. Resistance in the south lasted for decades until Taiwan was conquered in 1683.

title: Peace of Westphalia
summary: In Münster and Osnabrück the first great European peace congress brings the Thirty Years' War to an end.
text: After five years of negotiations, Catholics, Lutherans, and Calvinists in the empire received equal rights, and the territorial rulers gained far-reaching sovereignty. France and Sweden received territories, and the independence of the Netherlands and of Switzerland was recognized. The peace is regarded as the birth of the modern system of states, in which sovereign states regulate their relations by treaty.

title: Aurangzeb's rule over the Mughal Empire
summary: Aurangzeb brings the Mughal Empire to its greatest extent, but endless wars and religious tensions pave the way for its collapse.
text: In 1658 Aurangzeb prevailed in the struggle against his brothers and had his father Shah Jahan confined in Agra Fort until his death. As a devout Sunni he reintroduced the special tax on non-Muslims in 1679 and sponsored a compilation of Islamic law. He conquered the sultanates of Bijapur and Golconda in the Deccan, so that the empire covered almost the entire subcontinent. Against the Marathas under Shivaji and his successors, however, he waged war for decades. After his death in 1707 the empire disintegrated rapidly.

title: Founding of the Royal Society
summary: In London, scholars found a society for the advancement of scientific knowledge through experiment and exchange.
text: After a lecture by the architect Christopher Wren, twelve men, among them Robert Boyle, resolved on 28 November 1660 to form a society for the advancement of knowledge about nature; in 1662 it received a royal charter. Its motto Nullius in verba, on no one's word, expressed the principle that only experiment and observation should count as proof. From 1665 the Philosophical Transactions appeared, the oldest scientific journal still in existence, and Robert Hooke as curator demonstrated experiments every week. Newton headed the society from 1703 until his death; academies in Paris, Berlin, and St Petersburg were founded on its model.

title: Battle of Mbwila
summary: Portuguese troops from Angola defeat the army of the kingdom of Kongo and kill King António I.
text: In the 17th century relations between Kongo and the Portuguese colony of Angola deteriorated because of border disputes and the struggle over mineral resources. In October 1665 a battle took place at Mbwila, in which a Portuguese army with many African auxiliaries defeated the forces of Kongo. King António I was killed, and his head was taken to Luanda. In the following decades Kongo disintegrated in civil wars between rival noble families, in which many captives were drawn into the slave trade. Only at the beginning of the 18th century was the kingdom reunited, though with greatly diminished power.

title: Louis XIV moves the court to Versailles
summary: The Sun King makes the magnificent palace of Versailles the permanent seat of government and court.
text: Out of a hunting lodge belonging to his father, Louis XIV had an enormous complex built over decades, with the Hall of Mirrors and its gardens. The nobility was tied to the court, where it competed for the king's favor in a strictly regulated ceremonial and was thereby deprived of political power. Versailles became the model for palaces throughout Europe and a symbol of absolutism.

title: The second siege of Vienna by the Ottomans
summary: A relief army under the Polish king John III Sobieski defeats the Ottoman army before Vienna and begins the Ottoman withdrawal from central Europe.
text: In July 1683 the grand vizier Kara Mustafa encircled Vienna with around 150,000 men, and the garrison and citizens held the city for two months while Emperor Leopold I had fled. On 12 September an army of imperial, Polish, Bavarian, and Saxon troops attacked down from the Kahlenberg; the charge of the Polish cavalry decided the battle. In the Great Turkish War that followed, the Habsburgs conquered Hungary and Transylvania, which the Treaty of Karlowitz confirmed in 1699. Austria thus became a great power in southeastern Europe, and Ottoman expansion in Europe was at an end.

title: Edict of Fontainebleau: the expulsion of the Huguenots
summary: Louis XIV revokes the Edict of Nantes and forbids Protestant worship in France; hundreds of thousands of Huguenots flee.
text: For the Sun King, the unity of the state included the unity of faith, and even before 1685 billeted dragoons had forced Protestant families to convert. The edict of October 1685 had the churches of the Huguenots torn down, banished their pastors, and at the same time forbade the faithful to emigrate. Nevertheless some 200,000 people fled, many of them craftsmen, merchants, and officers, to the Netherlands, England, Switzerland, and Brandenburg, which invited them with the Edict of Potsdam. France lost valuable skilled workers, and the thinkers of the Enlightenment saw in the edict an example of the consequences of religious intolerance.

title: Newton publishes the Principia
summary: With the laws of motion and the law of gravitation, Isaac Newton founds classical physics.
text: In the Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica, Newton showed that the same force makes an apple fall to the ground and holds the moon in its orbit. The movements of the planets, the tides, and the trajectory of projectiles could now be calculated with a few mathematical laws. The work became the model for a science that understands nature as governed by law and open to calculation.

title: The flowering of Genroku culture in Japan
summary: In the cities of the Edo period a lively urban culture emerges with kabuki, puppet theatre, haiku, novels and woodblock prints.
text: The long peace under the Tokugawa allowed cities such as Edo, Osaka and Kyoto to grow, and wealthy merchants there developed a lifestyle of their own. In the Genroku period Ihara Saikaku wrote novels about love and money, and Chikamatsu Monzaemon wrote plays for puppet theatre and kabuki. Matsuo Bashō made the short haiku poem a recognized art and in 1689 walked to the north of Japan. Artists began to print pictures of the floating world of the pleasure quarters as woodblock prints. This art form influenced European painters in the 19th century.

title: The Glorious Revolution in England
summary: The English parliament drives out the Catholic king James II and establishes the supremacy of parliament.
text: Parliament called the Protestant William of Orange and his wife Mary into the country, whereupon James II fled to France almost without a fight. In 1689 the new rulers had to accept the Bill of Rights, which secured for parliament the right to grant taxes, free elections, and freedom of speech. England thus became a constitutional monarchy and a counter-model to absolutism.

title: Locke publishes the Two Treatises of Government
summary: John Locke bases rule on the consent of the governed and on the protection of life, liberty, and property.
text: Shortly after the Glorious Revolution, Locke's Two Treatises of Government appeared anonymously, in which he refuted the doctrine of the divine right of kings. Human beings, he argued, are by nature free and equal and join together in a state only in order to secure their natural rights; a government that violates these rights may be removed. In the same year his Letter Concerning Toleration appeared, and his Essay Concerning Human Understanding, which traced all knowledge back to experience. Locke's ideas shaped the American Declaration of Independence and liberal political theory to this day.

title: Treaty of Nerchinsk
summary: After border fighting on the Amur, Russia and Qing China fix their border by treaty for the first time.
text: Russian Cossacks had built forts such as Albazin on the Amur, which were besieged by troops of the Kangxi emperor. In 1689 envoys of both empires negotiated at Nerchinsk east of Lake Baikal; Jesuits served as interpreters, and the binding text was drawn up in Latin. Russia gave up the Amur region and in return received the right to trade with China. The treaty was the first that China concluded with a European state on an equal footing. The border held until the middle of the 19th century.

title: Sor Juana's “Reply to Sor Filotea”
summary: The Mexican nun and poet Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz defends the right of women to knowledge and study.
text: In 1690 the Bishop of Puebla had published a theological text by Sor Juana and, under the pseudonym Sor Filotea, at the same time admonished her to devote herself to pious rather than worldly studies. In her reply of 1691 Sor Juana described her lifelong thirst for knowledge and invoked learned women of the Bible and of antiquity. She argued that education did not lead women away from faith but deepened it. The text is regarded as one of the earliest writings in the Americas to justify the right of women to education. A few years later Sor Juana gave up her library.

title: Gold rush in Minas Gerais
summary: Gold finds in the interior of Brazil set off a wave of migration and shift the colony's centre of gravity to the south.
text: In the 1690s bandeirantes from São Paulo found rich gold deposits in the mountains of what later became Minas Gerais. Tens of thousands of Portuguese and Brazilians moved to the new mining towns such as Vila Rica, today's Ouro Preto, and large numbers of enslaved Africans were brought with them into the mines. In the 18th century diamond finds followed. Much of the gold flowed via Portugal to England. In 1763 the capital was moved from Salvador to Rio de Janeiro, the port of the gold region.

title: Treaty of Karlowitz
summary: After the Great Turkish War the Ottoman Empire cedes Hungary and Transylvania to the Habsburgs – the beginning of the retreat from central Europe.
text: After the failed siege of Vienna in 1683, the Habsburgs, Poland, Venice and Russia had fought the Ottomans in the Holy League; Prince Eugene won at Zenta in 1697. On 26 January 1699 peace was concluded at Karlowitz in Syrmia. The Habsburgs received almost all of Hungary and Transylvania, Venice the Peloponnese and Poland Podolia. For the first time the Ottomans accepted the mediation of foreign envoys and fixed borders. The treaty marks the end of Ottoman expansion in Europe.

title: Osei Tutu founds the Asante Empire
summary: With the victory over Denkyira at Feyiase and the symbol of the Golden Stool, Osei Tutu unites the Akan states into the Asante Empire.
text: In the late 17th century several Akan states in the forest zone of present-day Ghana joined together under Osei Tutu, the ruler of Kumasi. According to tradition, the priest Okomfo Anokye caused a golden stool to descend from the sky, which from then on embodied the soul and unity of the people. Around 1701 the Asante defeated the kingdom of Denkyira, to which they had until then paid tribute, at Feyiase. Osei Tutu became the first asantehene, and Kumasi developed into the capital of an empire that traded in gold, kola nuts and captives. Asante remained one of the strongest powers in West Africa until the late 19th century.

title: Peter the Great founds St Petersburg
summary: In the marshland on the Neva, the tsar has a new capital built as a window on Europe.
text: During the Great Northern War against Sweden, Peter I laid out the Peter and Paul Fortress on conquered land by the Baltic, and from it the city grew. Tens of thousands of forced laborers died during the building work on the marshy ground. In 1712 St Petersburg became the capital of Russia and remained so until 1918; the city symbolized the opening of the empire to the west.

title: The Tulip Period
summary: Under Ahmed III and his grand vizier Damad İbrahim Pasha, Istanbul experiences a time of peace full of festivities, gardens and curiosity about Europe.
text: After the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718 the grand vizier Nevşehirli Damad İbrahim Pasha relied on diplomacy and splendour. Palaces and gardens such as Sadabad arose on the Golden Horn, tulip bulbs became coveted luxury goods, and the court celebrated festivals of lights. An envoy reported from Paris on Versailles in 1720/21, and in 1727 the first press for Turkish books was set up. The extravagance and new taxes aroused discontent: in 1730 the revolt of Patrona Halil toppled the grand vizier and Sultan Ahmed III. The name "Tulip Period" was only coined by writers of the 20th century.

title: Dahomey conquers the slave port of Ouidah
summary: King Agaja of Dahomey conquers the coastal town of Ouidah and secures direct trade with the Europeans for his kingdom.
text: Dahomey, with its capital Abomey, lay in the hinterland of the so-called Slave Coast in present-day Benin. King Agaja conquered the kingdom of Allada in 1724 and in 1727 the port of Ouidah, one of the most important hubs of the Atlantic slave trade. Dahomey sold prisoners of war to European traders and received firearms, cloth and cowrie shells in return. The state was tightly organized, and a corps of female warriors, called Amazons by Europeans, formed part of its army. Until the 19th century hundreds of thousands of people were carried off from Ouidah to the Americas.

title: Müteferrika founds the first Turkish printing press
summary: İbrahim Müteferrika receives the sultan's permission to print books in Ottoman Turkish with Arabic type.
text: Jewish printers had been working in the empire since the late 15th century, Armenian and Greek printers since the 16th and 17th centuries, but books in Arabic script continued to be copied by hand. In 1727 İbrahim Müteferrika and Said Efendi received a decree from the sultan and an approving opinion from the şeyhülislam; religious texts remained excluded. In 1729 the first book appeared, an Arabic-Turkish dictionary. By 1742 Müteferrika had printed 17 works, among them histories, maps and a treatise on military reform. A broad book market only emerged in the 19th century.

title: Oyo forces Dahomey to pay tribute
summary: After several campaigns by its cavalry, the Yoruba empire of Oyo makes the kingdom of Dahomey its tributary.
text: Oyo, in the savanna north of the rainforest, was the most powerful Yoruba state in the 17th and 18th centuries. Its strength rested on a large cavalry whose horses were imported from the north. After repeated invasions of Dahomey, King Agaja had to recognize Oyo's overlordship around 1730 and pay annual tribute. The alaafin, the king of Oyo, ruled together with a council of nobles, the Oyo Mesi, which could even force him to commit suicide. In the early 19th century Oyo broke apart through internal power struggles and attacks from the north.

title: The Qianlong Emperor and the height of the Qing dynasty
summary: Under the Qianlong Emperor, China reaches its greatest extent and a golden age of culture.
text: Qianlong reigned from 1735 to 1796 and extended the empire through campaigns into Central Asia, Tibet, and the southwest. The population grew to around 300 million, and the emperor had an enormous collection of Chinese literature compiled. Toward European wishes for trade, China remained closed; in 1793 Qianlong turned away a British embassy with the remark that his empire had no need of foreign goods.

title: Maria Theresa and the War of the Austrian Succession
summary: After the death of Emperor Charles VI, Prussia, Bavaria, and France attack the inheritance of the 23-year-old Maria Theresa, who holds on to her lands except for Silesia.
text: Charles VI had secured his daughter's succession with the Pragmatic Sanction, but he had hardly died in October 1740 when Frederick II of Prussia invaded the wealthy province of Silesia, and Bavaria and France put forward claims of their own. Maria Theresa won the support of the Hungarian estates, raised new armies, and in 1745 secured the election of her husband Francis Stephen as emperor. The Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle in 1748 confirmed her possessions but left Silesia with Prussia. From the defeat she drew the conclusion that the administration, army, taxes, and school system of her lands had to be fundamentally reformed.

title: Montesquieu publishes The Spirit of the Laws
summary: Charles de Montesquieu calls for the separation of legislative, executive, and judicial power in order to secure liberty against the abuse of power.
text: The baron from Bordeaux had spent twenty years comparing the constitutions, climates, customs, and laws of different peoples, and had traveled in England. In his work, printed in Geneva, he described the English constitution as a model, because there the king, parliament, and independent courts limited one another; where all power lies in one hand, he wrote, there is no liberty. He distinguished between republic, monarchy, and despotism and warned against arbitrary rule. Although the church placed the book on the Index in 1751, it was read throughout Europe and influenced the Constitution of the United States of 1787 as well as the French revolutionaries.

title: The first volumes of the Encyclopédie appear
summary: Denis Diderot and Jean le Rond d'Alembert publish the first volume of the great encyclopedia of the Enlightenment in Paris.
text: The Encyclopédie was to gather the entire knowledge of the age, from philosophy to the crafts, and make it accessible to reason. More than 140 authors, among them Voltaire, Rousseau, and Montesquieu, wrote articles that often criticized the church and absolutism in veiled form. Despite bans and censorship, the work grew by 1772 to 28 volumes with more than 70,000 articles and was read throughout Europe.

title: The Lisbon earthquake
summary: On All Saints' Day, an earthquake, a tidal wave, and fires destroy the Portuguese capital and set off a debate across Europe about God and nature.
text: On the morning of 1 November 1755, when the churches were full, a tremendous earthquake shook Lisbon; tidal waves flooded the harbor, and fires raged for days. Estimates range from 30,000 to 60,000 dead, and one of the richest cities in Europe lay in ruins. The minister Pombal organized rescue and reconstruction with earthquake-resistant buildings and had the causes investigated scientifically. In a poem and in Candide, Voltaire mocked the idea that everything in the world is ordered for the best, Rousseau contradicted him, and Kant wrote three treatises on the natural causes of earthquakes.

title: The Seven Years' War
summary: Prussia and Great Britain fight against Austria, France, and Russia in a war waged in Europe, America, and India.
text: Frederick II of Prussia opened the war with the invasion of Saxony and held his own against superior forces, but he came close to defeat several times; the death of the Russian tsarina Elizabeth in 1762 saved him. In North America and India, Great Britain defeated France and took over Canada as well as supremacy in Bengal. Prussia kept Silesia and rose to become a European great power.

title: Expulsion of the Jesuits from Spanish America
summary: King Charles III has the Jesuits expelled from all Spanish lands; the Guaraní reductions decline.
text: To the enlightened ministers of the Bourbons the Jesuit order seemed too powerful, too rich and too bound to the pope; Portugal had already banished it from its empire in 1759. In the summer of 1767 more than two thousand Jesuits in Spanish America were arrested and shipped to Europe. Their schools, haciendas and missions passed to the Crown or to other orders. In Mexico there were protests, which were violently suppressed. Many expelled Creole Jesuits wrote works on the history of their American homeland in exile in Italy.

title: James Cook's Pacific voyages
summary: On three voyages James Cook surveys New Zealand, the east coast of Australia, and countless islands of the Pacific, and ends the search for the southern continent.
text: On the commission of the Royal Society, Cook observed the transit of Venus on Tahiti in 1769, then sailed around New Zealand and in 1770 landed in Botany Bay on the east coast of Australia, which he claimed for Great Britain. On the second voyage he was the first to cross the Antarctic Circle and proved that there was no habitable southern continent; on the third he reached Hawaii, where he was killed in a dispute with local people in 1779. With a chronometer, sauerkraut against scurvy, and naturalists such as Joseph Banks and Georg Forster on board, his voyages turned exploration into a science. For the inhabitants of Australia and the Pacific islands, European colonization began with them.

title: James Watt improves the steam engine
summary: The Scottish instrument maker James Watt receives a patent for a steam engine with a separate condenser.
text: Thomas Newcomen's steam engine had been used since 1712 to pump water out of mines, but it consumed enormous quantities of coal. Watt recognized that the steam should be condensed in a separate vessel so that the cylinder stays hot; this reduced fuel consumption by about three quarters. Together with the entrepreneur Matthew Boulton he built engines from 1775 onward that soon drove factories, mills, and mines.

title: Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca
summary: After a heavy defeat by Russia, the Ottoman Empire loses its suzerainty over the Crimea and opens the Black Sea to Russian ships.
text: In the Russo-Ottoman War from 1768 the armies of Catherine the Great had defeated the Ottomans on the Danube and in 1770 destroyed their fleet at Çeşme. On 21 July 1774 peace was concluded in the Bulgarian village of Küçük Kaynarca. The Crimean Khanate became independent and was annexed by Russia in 1783; Russian merchant ships were allowed to sail the Black Sea and the Straits. Russia later derived a right of protection over the Orthodox Christians from the treaty. At the same time the sultan, as caliph, was named for the first time in a treaty as religious head of the Muslims.

title: The American Declaration of Independence
summary: On 4 July 1776, thirteen British colonies declare themselves the independent United States of America.
text: The dispute with London over taxes and representation had turned into open fighting in 1775. The text, written by Thomas Jefferson, justified the separation by the inalienable rights of all people to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. After the victory at Yorktown in 1781, Great Britain recognized independence in 1783; in 1787 the states gave themselves a federal constitution.

title: The uprising of Túpac Amaru II
summary: An Indigenous cacique from the region of Cusco leads the largest uprising against Spanish colonial rule in the 18th century.
text: José Gabriel Condorcanqui, who named himself after the last Inca ruler Túpac Amaru, had a hated colonial official arrested and executed in November 1780. He demanded the abolition of the mita and of the forced sales through which officials exploited the population. Tens of thousands of Indigenous people and mestizos joined him; his wife Micaela Bastidas organised supplies and troops. In April 1781 both were captured, and in May they were cruelly executed in Cusco. The uprising continued in the highlands until 1782 and cost tens of thousands of lives.

title: The power loom and the factory system
summary: Spinning machines and the power loom move textile production out of the home and into the factory.
text: With James Hargreaves's spinning jenny of the 1760s, one worker could operate several spindles at once, Richard Arkwright's water frame used water power from 1769, and in 1785 Edmund Cartwright patented the power loom. Because the machines were tied to a central source of power, large factories arose such as Arkwright's mill at Cromford, in which hundreds of people worked to fixed hours and under supervision. The handloom weavers could not compete with the cheap factory cloth and fell into poverty. The factory system spread from the cotton industry to all branches of industry and has shaped the world of work to this day.

title: The Constitution of the United States
summary: In Philadelphia the delegates of the states adopt the first modern written constitution, with a separation of powers and an elected president.
text: After the War of Independence the thirteen states formed only a loose confederation without powers of taxation or trade, which led to debt, unrest, and quarrels. From May to September 1787, 55 delegates under the chairmanship of George Washington deliberated on a new order in Philadelphia behind closed doors; James Madison is regarded as its most important architect. The constitution divided power between a Congress of two chambers, a president, and a Supreme Court, and between the federal government and the individual states; a compromise counted enslaved people as three fifths for the allocation of seats and thereby entrenched slavery. After fierce debates it came into force in 1789, and in 1791 ten amendments, the Bill of Rights, added basic rights such as freedom of speech, of the press, and of religion. The constitution remains in force, with amendments, to this day.

title: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen
summary: On 26 August 1789 the National Assembly proclaims liberty, equality, and the sovereignty of the people as basic rights.
text: In 17 articles the assembly declared that all human beings are born free and equal in rights, that all state power proceeds from the people, and that freedom of opinion and of religion, property, and protection against arbitrary treatment are to be guaranteed. Women, slaves, and those without property remained excluded at first; in 1791 Olympe de Gouges responded with a Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen. The declaration became a model for constitutions all over the world.

title: The Women's March on Versailles
summary: Thousands of Parisian women march to Versailles because of the shortage of bread and force the royal family to move to Paris.
text: In the autumn of 1789 the price of bread rose in Paris, while the king had still not confirmed the resolutions of the National Assembly, and rumors of a banquet held by the guard at Versailles increased the anger. On 5 October some 7,000 women of the market halls, armed with pikes and kitchen knives, marched the twenty kilometers to Versailles in the rain; the National Guard under Lafayette followed them. After the palace was stormed during the night, in which members of the bodyguard were killed, Louis XVI had to sign the Declaration of the Rights of Man and move with his family to the Tuileries in Paris, where the National Assembly followed as well. From then on the king stood before the eyes of the people, and women had shown themselves to be a political force of the revolution.

title: The storming of the Bastille
summary: On 14 July 1789 the people of Paris storm the royal prison, marking the beginning of the French Revolution.
text: After the Third Estate had declared itself the National Assembly and the king had gathered troops around Paris, the population armed itself. The Bastille held only a few prisoners but was regarded as a symbol of royal arbitrariness. Its fall forced Louis XVI to give way; throughout the country peasants rose against their landlords, and in August the National Assembly abolished feudal rights.

title: The beginning of the Haitian Revolution
summary: In the French colony of Saint-Domingue, the enslaved rise up against their masters.
text: Through its sugar and coffee plantations, Saint-Domingue was the richest colony of France, in which half a million slaves worked under cruel conditions. The uprising of August 1791 grew under the leadership of Toussaint Louverture into a war lasting years, in which the insurgents held their own against the French, the Spanish, and the British. In 1794 France abolished slavery; after Napoleon's attempt to reintroduce it, Haiti declared its independence in 1804.

title: Macartney's embassy to the court of Qianlong
summary: A British embassy under Lord Macartney asks the Qianlong emperor in vain for better trading conditions and a permanent mission in Beijing.
text: Britain bought large quantities of tea in China but was only allowed to trade in Canton under strict rules. In 1793 Qianlong received the envoy George Macartney at his summer residence in Chengde, where Macartney bent only one knee instead of performing the full kowtow. Macartney presented gifts such as astronomical instruments and asked for additional ports and a permanent embassy. In an edict to King George III the emperor rejected all the requests, saying that China had no need of foreign goods. The failed contact became a prelude to later conflicts.

title: The execution of Louis XVI and the Reign of Terror
summary: The king is guillotined, and the Committee of Public Safety under Robespierre establishes the rule of terror.
text: After his failed attempt to flee and the fall of the monarchy, Louis XVI was condemned for treason and executed on 21 January 1793. War against almost all of Europe, uprisings in the Vendée, and shortages of supplies led to the dictatorship of the Committee of Public Safety; by the summer of 1794 revolutionary tribunals had around 17,000 people executed, among them Queen Marie-Antoinette and Olympe de Gouges. In July 1794 Robespierre himself was overthrown and guillotined.

title: Selim III and the "New Order"
summary: Sultan Selim III raises an army trained on European lines and fails because of the resistance of the Janissaries.
text: After costly wars against Russia and Austria, Selim III had a new corps raised from 1793 that was trained by European officers and paid from a separate treasury. The "New Order" (Nizam-ı Cedid) also included engineering schools and the first permanent embassies in London, Paris, Vienna and Berlin. The Janissaries and parts of the clergy saw their position threatened. In 1807 a revolt toppled the sultan, who was murdered in 1808. His cousin Mahmud II later continued the reforms.

title: France abolishes slavery
summary: On 4 February 1794 the National Convention abolishes slavery in all French colonies, under the pressure of the uprising in Saint-Domingue.
text: Despite the Declaration of the Rights of Man, the National Assembly had at first left slavery in the colonies untouched, because planters and port cities profited from the sugar trade. Only the uprising in Saint-Domingue and the war against Spain and Great Britain forced the commissioners of the republic in 1793 to declare the enslaved free, in order to win them as soldiers. When a delegation from the colony, including the former slave Jean-Baptiste Belley, appeared before the Convention in February 1794, it resolved without a dissenting vote to abolish slavery in all colonies and to grant citizenship to all men regardless of the color of their skin. Napoleon reintroduced slavery in 1802, which rekindled the struggle for freedom in Haiti; France abolished it for good only in 1848.

title: Napoleon's Egyptian campaign
summary: Napoleon occupies Egypt in order to strike at Great Britain's route to India; the campaign fails, but it founds the modern study of ancient Egypt.
text: In July 1798 Napoleon landed in Egypt with 35,000 soldiers; the country formally belonged to the Ottoman Empire but was ruled by the Mamluks, and he defeated their cavalry at the Battle of the Pyramids. A few days later the British fleet under Nelson destroyed the French ships at Aboukir, so that the army was cut off from supplies; an advance into Syria failed before Acre in 1799. Napoleon left his army secretly in order to seize power in Paris; the remnants surrendered to the British in 1801. The 167 scholars who had accompanied him surveyed temples, pyramids, and wildlife and published their results in the Description de l'Égypte; the Rosetta Stone, found in 1799, enabled Champollion to decipher the hieroglyphs in 1822. In Egypt itself the campaign set in motion the rise of Muhammad Ali and the modernization of the country.

title: The Code civil comes into force
summary: Napoleon gives France a uniform civil code that establishes equality before the law and freedom of property.
text: The Code civil replaced hundreds of regional legal systems with a single code of more than 2,000 articles. It guaranteed the equality of all men before the law, freedom of contract and of trade, private property, and civil marriage, but it placed women under the guardianship of father or husband. It was introduced in the territories ruled by France, such as the Rhineland, the Netherlands, and Italy, and in part remained in force into the 20th century.

title: Napoleon crowns himself emperor
summary: In the cathedral of Notre-Dame, Napoleon Bonaparte places the imperial crown on his own head on 2 December 1804.
text: After the coup of 1799, Napoleon had stabilized France as First Consul and had himself confirmed by plebiscite. Pope Pius VII was present at the coronation, but Napoleon crowned himself and then his wife Joséphine, in order to show that he owed his power to no one. As Emperor of the French he led Europe into a decade of wars and reshaped the continent according to his will.

title: The independence of Haiti
summary: On 1 January 1804 Jean-Jacques Dessalines declares the independence of Haiti, the first state founded by formerly enslaved people.
text: After Napoleon had sent an army to Saint-Domingue in 1802 to restore slavery, and after Toussaint Louverture had been carried off into captivity, Jean-Jacques Dessalines and Alexandre Pétion carried on the resistance. Yellow fever and the guerrilla warfare of the former slaves wore down the French troops; after the defeat at Vertières in November 1803 the French evacuated the colony. On 1 January 1804 Dessalines proclaimed independence at Gonaïves and gave the country its old indigenous name, Haiti; massacres of the remaining French followed. Haiti became the second independent state in the Americas, but it remained isolated by the slaveholding powers; France recognized it only in 1825, in return for an indemnity of 150 million francs that burdened the country for more than a century.

title: Usman dan Fodio's jihad and the Sokoto Caliphate
summary: The Fulani scholar Usman dan Fodio overthrows the Hausa kings and founds the Sokoto Caliphate, the largest state in West Africa in the 19th century.
text: In the Hausa state of Gobir, Usman dan Fodio preached against the taxation, arbitrary rule and, in his view, imperfect Islam of the rulers.
