In the summer of 1942, after the capture of Tobruk, Rommel stood only 100 kilometers from Alexandria, but his supply lines were overextended, and Allied aircraft and submarines sank his tankers in the Mediterranean. The new British commander Bernard Montgomery attacked on 23 October 1942 with roughly twice the strength in soldiers, tanks and aircraft, including troops from Australia, New Zealand, India and South Africa; after twelve days the German-Italian front broke, and Rommel withdrew to the west in defiance of an order from Hitler to hold. A few days later American and British troops landed in Morocco and Algeria; in May 1943 around 250,000 Axis soldiers surrendered in Tunisia. Churchill called El Alamein the end of the beginning.

title: Battle of Stalingrad
summary: The encirclement and destruction of the Sixth Army on the Volga is regarded as the turning point of the war in Europe.
text: In the summer of 1942 the Wehrmacht advanced as far as the Volga and fought in bitter street battles for the city of Stalingrad. In November the Red Army encircled the German troops; Hitler forbade a breakout. After hunger, cold and fighting, the remnants of the Sixth Army surrendered on 2 February 1943. About 150,000 German soldiers had been killed and around 90,000 were taken prisoner, of whom only about 6,000 returned. After that the Wehrmacht was permanently on the defensive in the east.

title: Wannsee Conference
summary: Senior officials and SS leaders coordinate the deportation and murder of all European Jews.
text: On 20 January 1942 fifteen representatives of the SS, the party and the ministries met under the chairmanship of Reinhard Heydrich in a villa on the Wannsee in Berlin. The conference did not decide on the genocide, since mass murder had already been under way for months, but organized the cooperation of the authorities in the so-called Final Solution of the Jewish Question. The minutes named eleven million Jews across the whole of Europe as the target group. In the months that followed, the deportations to the extermination camps of Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau began.

title: Warsaw Ghetto Uprising
summary: The last inhabitants of the ghetto put up armed resistance to the SS for almost four weeks, choosing to fight rather than be deported.
text: In the Warsaw ghetto, which the German occupation had sealed off with a wall in 1940, more than 400,000 people lived crammed into the narrowest of spaces, and tens of thousands of them died of hunger and disease. Between July and September 1942 the SS deported about 265,000 inhabitants to the Treblinka extermination camp. The remaining 60,000 or so now knew what deportation meant; young people joined together in the Jewish Combat Organization under the 24-year-old Mordechai Anielewicz and in the Jewish Military Union, laboriously procuring pistols and homemade firebombs. When the SS moved in on 19 April 1943 for the final clearance, it came under fire and had to withdraw. The SS commander Jürgen Stroop thereupon had the ghetto burned down and blown up house by house; on 8 May Anielewicz and his comrades died in the bunker on Miła Street, and on 16 May, after the demolition of the Great Synagogue, Stroop reported that the ghetto no longer existed. About 7,000 people had died in the fighting, and the survivors were deported to Treblinka and Majdanek. The uprising was the first large armed revolt in an occupied city and became a symbol of Jewish resistance.

title: Assassination Attempt of 20 July 1944
summary: Stauffenberg's bomb misses Hitler, the coup fails, and the regime takes revenge with hundreds of executions.
text: A circle of officers, diplomats, trade unionists and politicians had been planning for years to remove Hitler and end the war before Germany was completely destroyed. On 20 July 1944 Colonel Claus Schenk Graf von Stauffenberg detonated a bomb in a briefcase during a situation conference at the Wolf's Lair headquarters in East Prussia. Four men died, but Hitler was only slightly injured because the briefcase had been pushed behind a massive table support. Stauffenberg flew to Berlin and, with his fellow conspirators in the Bendlerblock, set in motion the Valkyrie plan, under which the Replacement Army was to take power; when word spread that Hitler had survived, the coup collapsed. Stauffenberg, Friedrich Olbricht, Albrecht Mertz von Quirnheim and Werner von Haeften were shot in the courtyard that same night. In the following months the People's Court under Roland Freisler sentenced around 200 people to death, among them Helmuth James von Moltke, Carl Goerdeler and Julius Leber; their relatives were taken into kin liability detention. Today 20 July is regarded as a symbol of the fact that even among the leading class of the Reich there were people who placed their conscience above obedience.

title: D-Day in Normandy
summary: With the largest landing operation in history, the Western Allies open the second front in France.
text: On 6 June 1944 more than 150,000 American, British and Canadian soldiers landed on five stretches of beach in Normandy, supported by almost 7,000 ships and 11,000 aircraft. Despite heavy losses, above all at Omaha Beach, a bridgehead was successfully established. By the end of August Paris had been liberated, and the Wehrmacht had to withdraw to the German border. At the same time the Soviet summer offensive smashed the German Army Group Centre.

title: Atomic Bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki
summary: The United States uses nuclear weapons for the first time; Japan surrenders and the Second World War is over.
text: On 6 August 1945 the atomic bomb Little Boy destroyed the city of Hiroshima, and on 9 August Fat Man struck Nagasaki. By the end of 1945 more than 200,000 people had died from the explosion, the fires and the radiation. President Truman wanted to avoid a costly invasion of Japan; at the same time the Soviet Union declared war on Japan. On 15 August Emperor Hirohito announced the surrender, which was signed on 2 September. The atomic age had begun.

title: Liberation of Auschwitz
summary: Soviet soldiers reach the largest extermination camp of the National Socialists on 27 January 1945.
text: At Auschwitz-Birkenau in occupied Poland the SS had murdered more than 1.1 million people between 1940 and 1945, among them around one million Jews, as well as Poles, Sinti and Roma and Soviet prisoners of war. Shortly before the liberation the SS drove about 60,000 prisoners westward on death marches; the soldiers of the Red Army found around 7,000 exhausted survivors, among them many children. Today 27 January is the international day of remembrance for the victims of the Holocaust.

title: Founding of the United Nations
summary: 51 states sign the Charter of the United Nations in San Francisco.
text: While the war was still going on, the Allies had prepared a new world organization that was to be stronger than the failed League of Nations. The charter was signed on 26 June 1945 and came into force on 24 October. The Security Council, with its five permanent members the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain, France and China, received the right to decide on sanctions and military operations. In 1948 the General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

title: Surrender of Germany
summary: With the unconditional surrender of the Wehrmacht on 8 May 1945 the war in Europe comes to an end.
text: After the Red Army had captured Berlin and Hitler had taken his own life in the bunker of the Reich Chancellery on 30 April, the leadership of the Wehrmacht signed the unconditional surrender on 7 May in Reims and on 8 May in Berlin-Karlshorst. Germany was divided into four occupation zones, and the major war criminals were indicted before the Nuremberg tribunal. In Germany today 8 May is understood as the day of liberation from National Socialism.

title: Nuremberg Trials
summary: For the first time the leaders of a state have to answer before an international court for waging a war of aggression and for crimes against humanity.
text: In the summer of 1945 the four victorious powers agreed not to shoot those chiefly responsible for the Nazi regime by summary justice, but to charge them in proceedings under the rule of law. From 20 November 1945 to 1 October 1946 the International Military Tribunal sat in the Palace of Justice in Nuremberg and tried 24 defendants, among them Hermann Göring, Rudolf Hess, Joachim von Ribbentrop and Albert Speer, for conspiracy, crimes against peace, war crimes and crimes against humanity. The evidence consisted above all of the perpetrators' own files, together with films from the liberated camps and testimony from survivors; the objection that they had only been following orders was not accepted as an excuse. Twelve defendants were sentenced to death, Göring escaped execution by taking poison, and three were acquitted. In twelve subsequent trials up to 1949, doctors, lawyers, industrialists, diplomats and commanders of the Einsatzgruppen stood before American courts, and in Tokyo a parallel tribunal tried the Japanese leadership. The Nuremberg Principles became the foundation of international criminal law and of the International Criminal Court.

title: Independence of India and Pakistan
summary: British India becomes independent and is divided into the states of India and Pakistan.
text: After decades of nonviolent resistance under Mahatma Gandhi, Britain released its most important colony into independence on 15 August 1947. Because Hindus and Muslims could not agree on a common state, the country was divided into predominantly Hindu India and Muslim Pakistan. Up to 15 million people fled across the new borders, and hundreds of thousands died in massacres. The dispute over Kashmir still burdens relations between the two nuclear powers today.

title: Berlin Airlift
summary: After the Soviet blockade of West Berlin, the Western powers supply the city from the air for almost a year.
text: When the Western powers introduced the deutschmark in their zones in June 1948, the Soviet Union closed all roads, railways and waterways to West Berlin in order to push the Western Allies out of the city. The United States and Britain thereupon set up an airlift: in almost 280,000 flights the raisin bombers brought around 2.3 million tons of coal, food and medicine to the roughly two million Berliners. On 12 May 1949 Stalin lifted the blockade. The airlift turned the occupiers into protectors in the eyes of many Germans, led to the founding of NATO in 1949 and accelerated the emergence of the Federal Republic and the GDR in the same year.

title: Founding of Israel
summary: David Ben-Gurion proclaims the State of Israel; the first Arab-Israeli war begins.
text: In 1947 the United Nations had decided to partition the British mandate territory of Palestine into a Jewish and an Arab state. On 14 May 1948 Ben-Gurion proclaimed the independence of Israel, which after the Holocaust offered a home to many survivors. The neighboring Arab states attacked at once, Israel held its ground and enlarged its territory. Around 700,000 Palestinians fled or were driven out; the refugee question and the borders remain at the heart of the Middle East conflict to this day.

title: Proclamation of the People's Republic of China
summary: After victory in the civil war, Mao Zedong proclaims the People's Republic in Beijing.
text: The civil war between Mao's communists and the nationalists under Chiang Kai-shek ended in 1949 with the withdrawal of the nationalists to Taiwan. On 1 October Mao proclaimed the founding of the People's Republic from the Gate of Heavenly Peace. The communists distributed the land to the peasants and built up a planned economy on the Soviet model. Mao's campaigns such as the Great Leap Forward and the Cultural Revolution later cost millions of people their lives.

title: Korean War
summary: North Korea's attack on the South leads to the first hot war of the Cold War, with millions of dead.
text: In 1945 Korea had been divided along the 38th parallel into a Soviet and an American zone, out of which two hostile states emerged. On 25 June 1950 communist North Korea attacked the South with Stalin's approval; the United Nations, from whose Security Council the Soviet Union was absent at the time, sent troops under American command. After the landing at Incheon the UN forces advanced as far as the Chinese border, whereupon China intervened with hundreds of thousands of soldiers. The armistice of 1953 restored the old border; a peace treaty was never concluded. Around three million people died, and Korea remains divided to this day.

title: Bandung Conference
summary: 29 Asian and African states meet in Indonesia and call for a path of their own between the blocs.
text: At the invitation of Indonesia, India, Pakistan, Burma and Ceylon, representatives of 29 states, together representing more than half of the world's population, came together in Bandung in April 1955. Jawaharlal Nehru, Sukarno, Gamal Abdel Nasser and China's prime minister Zhou Enlai condemned colonialism and racism, called for respect for sovereignty and rejected alignment with the military blocs. For the first time the conference gave the decolonized countries a common voice in world politics. Out of it grew the Non-Aligned Movement in Belgrade in 1961, which still exists today.

title: Montgomery Bus Boycott
summary: The arrest of Rosa Parks sets off a boycott lasting 381 days and makes Martin Luther King the leader of the civil rights movement.
text: On 1 December 1955 the seamstress Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus to a white passenger in Montgomery, Alabama, and was arrested. The city's black community thereupon decided to stop using the buses; for more than a year tens of thousands walked or organized car pools. The 26-year-old pastor Martin Luther King led the boycott and became the spokesman of nonviolent resistance to racial segregation. In November 1956 the Supreme Court declared segregation on buses unconstitutional. The success encouraged sit-ins, freedom rides and the March on Washington in 1963, which led to the civil rights and voting rights acts of 1964 and 1965.

title: Launch of Sputnik 1
summary: The Soviet Union sends the first artificial satellite into space and triggers the Sputnik shock in the West.
text: On 4 October 1957 a Soviet rocket carried the 84-kilogram metal sphere Sputnik into orbit around the earth; radio amateurs all over the world could pick up its beeping. For the United States this was a shock, because the same rocket could carry nuclear warheads across the ocean, and the Soviet Union appeared to be technically superior. In 1958 Washington founded the space agency NASA and invested massively in science and education. The race into space brought the first human being into space with Yuri Gagarin in 1961, the American Moon landing in 1969, and satellites for weather, television and navigation.

title: The Year of Africa
summary: In a single year 17 African colonies become independent states.
text: After Ghana under Kwame Nkrumah had gained independence in 1957 as the first colony south of the Sahara, France in 1960 released almost all of its African territories from Senegal to Madagascar into independence; Nigeria, Somalia and the Belgian Congo also became independent. The United Nations admitted 17 new members and adopted a declaration against colonialism. But the borders of the colonial era, weak institutions and the interference of the superpowers weighed on the young states: in the Congo a civil war broke out immediately, in the course of which the first prime minister Patrice Lumumba was murdered in 1961. The settler colonies in the south, such as Algeria, Angola and Rhodesia, still had to win their freedom in long wars.

title: Building of the Berlin Wall
summary: On 13 August 1961 the GDR seals off West Berlin and puts an end to the flight of its citizens to the West.
text: By 1961 almost three million people had left the GDR by way of open Berlin. With Moscow's consent, the SED leadership under Walter Ulbricht had streets torn up and barbed wire strung during the night of 13 August; a concrete wall with a death strip soon followed. Families were separated overnight, and at least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall. It became the symbol of the Cold War and of the division of Europe.

title: Cuban Missile Crisis
summary: Soviet missiles in Cuba bring the world to the brink of nuclear war for thirteen days.
text: In October 1962 American reconnaissance aircraft discovered launch pads for Soviet medium-range missiles in Cuba. President Kennedy imposed a naval blockade and demanded their withdrawal. After days of tension Khrushchev gave in; in return the United States pledged not to attack Cuba and secretly withdrew missiles from Turkey. The crisis led to the establishment of the hotline between Washington and Moscow and, in 1963, to the first agreement on nuclear testing.

title: Vietnam War
summary: The United States intervenes in Vietnam with hundreds of thousands of soldiers and suffers its first defeat in a war.
text: After the victory of the Viet Minh over France in 1954, Vietnam was divided into a communist North under Ho Chi Minh and a South supported by the West. In order to halt the advance of communism in Southeast Asia, the United States sent ground troops from March 1965 onward and bombed the North; at the peak more than 500,000 American soldiers were in the country. Despite superior technology they were unable to defeat the Viet Cong guerrillas, and the television images of napalm and destroyed villages provoked protests worldwide. In 1973 the United States withdrew, and in 1975 the North took Saigon and united the country. Around 58,000 Americans and several million Vietnamese lost their lives.

title: Cultural Revolution in China
summary: Mao Zedong mobilizes the young against the party, intellectuals and traditions; terror and chaos grip the country.
text: In order to regain the power he had lost after the failed Great Leap Forward, Mao called on young people in 1966 to fight against bourgeois ideas and alleged traitors within the party. Millions of Red Guards waved the Little Red Book, publicly humiliated teachers, officials and artists, destroyed temples and books and deported the educated to the countryside for re-education; Deng Xiaoping too was stripped of power, and head of state Liu Shaoqi died in custody. Schools and universities remained closed for years, and the economy collapsed. Only Mao's death and the arrest of the Gang of Four in 1976 brought an end to the decade, which by some estimates cost more than a million lives. In 1981 the party declared it a catastrophe, but forbade any open examination of it.

title: Prague Spring and the Year of Protest 1968
summary: Warsaw Pact troops stifle the attempt at reform in Czechoslovakia, while in the West students rebel.
text: Under its new party leader Alexander Dubček, Czechoslovakia attempted from January 1968 to create a socialism with a human face: censorship was lifted, travel permitted and economic reforms begun. During the night of 21 August around half a million soldiers of the Soviet Union and its allies marched in; the population offered nonviolent resistance, but the reforms were reversed, and the Brezhnev Doctrine declared such intervention to be the rule. In the same year students protested in Paris, Berlin, Berkeley and Mexico City against the Vietnam War, authoritarian structures and the silence of their parents' generation. 1968 became the symbol of a generation of new departures that changed society, universities and political culture.

title: Moon Landing
summary: Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin become the first people to set foot on the Moon.
text: After the Soviet Union had led the race into space with Sputnik in 1957 and Yuri Gagarin in 1961, Kennedy promised to put a human being on the Moon before the end of the decade. On 20 July 1969 the lunar module of Apollo 11 landed; around 600 million people watched live as Armstrong stepped onto the Moon. Five further landings followed up to 1972. The program brought advances in computer technology, materials and communications.

title: Oil Crisis
summary: The Arab oil states cut production; prices quadruple, and the economic miracle comes to an end.
text: During the Yom Kippur War in October 1973 the Arab OPEC states used oil as a political weapon against the supporters of Israel. In Western Europe and the United States there were fuel shortages, car-free Sundays and speed limits; inflation and unemployment rose. The crisis brought the postwar boom to an end and put energy saving, nuclear power and renewable energies on the political agenda.

title: Iranian Revolution
summary: The overthrow of the Shah turns Iran into an Islamic republic under Ayatollah Khomeini.
text: In 1978 millions of Iranians took to the streets against the dictatorship, the westernization and the social inequality under Shah Mohammad Reza Pahlavi; clergy, students, merchants and the left united in protest. In January 1979 the Shah left the country, in February the cleric Ruhollah Khomeini returned from exile and had an Islamic republic proclaimed by referendum, in which the word of the supreme religious leader stands above all laws. The occupation of the American embassy in Tehran, with 444 days of hostage-taking, destroyed relations with the United States, and the Iraqi attack in 1980 led to an eight-year war. The revolution gave political Islam a boost worldwide and triggered the second oil crisis.

title: Chernobyl Nuclear Disaster
summary: The explosion of a Soviet nuclear reactor contaminates large parts of Europe with radiation and shakes confidence in nuclear power.
text: During a botched test on 26 April 1986, reactor block 4 of the Chernobyl nuclear power plant in Ukraine exploded; burning graphite hurled radioactive material kilometers into the air. The Soviet leadership kept silent for days, and only measurements in Sweden forced it to disclose what had happened; the town of Pripyat and a zone of 30 kilometers were evacuated, and hundreds of thousands of clean-up workers were exposed to high levels of radiation. The radioactive cloud came down over Belarus, Scandinavia and Central Europe, where playgrounds were closed off and vegetables destroyed. The disaster reinforced Gorbachev's policy of openness, strengthened the anti-nuclear movement and led several countries to phase out nuclear energy.

title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
summary: On 9 November 1989 the GDR opens the border; the peaceful revolution puts an end to the division of Germany.
text: Mass flight by way of Hungary and the Monday demonstrations in Leipzig put the SED leadership under pressure in the autumn of 1989. When politburo member Günter Schabowski announced new travel regulations on the evening of 9 November, tens of thousands streamed to the border crossings, and the border guards raised the barriers. The communist regimes also fell in Poland, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and Romania. On 3 October 1990 the GDR acceded to the Federal Republic.

title: Dissolution of the Soviet Union
summary: The Soviet Union breaks apart into fifteen independent states; the Cold War is over.
text: Gorbachev's reforms had created freedoms but had not solved the economic crisis; the Baltic republics and others demanded independence. In August 1991 a coup by communist hardliners failed against the resistance gathered around Boris Yeltsin. On 8 December Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declared the union dissolved, and on 25 December Gorbachev resigned. Russia took over the legacy of the Soviet Union, including its nuclear weapons and its seat on the Security Council.

title: The World Wide Web Goes Public
summary: Tim Berners-Lee puts the first website online at CERN and makes the internet usable for everyone.
text: Since the 1970s the internet had connected computers at universities and in the military, but it could be operated only by specialists. From 1989 onward the British physicist Tim Berners-Lee developed at the CERN research center near Geneva a system consisting of web addresses, the transfer protocol HTTP and the page language HTML, with which documents could be linked worldwide. In August 1991 he made the first website public, in 1993 CERN released the technology free of charge, and with the Mosaic browser its triumphal progress began. Within a few years search engines, online commerce and social networks came into being; today more than five billion people use the network, which has fundamentally changed the economy, politics and everyday life.

title: The Yugoslav Wars
summary: The break-up of Yugoslavia leads to the bloodiest wars in Europe since 1945, with expulsions and a genocide in Srebrenica.
text: After Tito's death and the end of communism, Slovenia and Croatia declared their independence in June 1991, and Bosnia and Herzegovina followed in 1992. Serbian nationalists under Slobodan Milošević sought to prevent this, and wars with mass expulsions, called ethnic cleansing, followed. Sarajevo was besieged for almost four years, and in July 1995 Bosnian Serb troops murdered around 8,000 Muslim men and boys in Srebrenica. The Dayton Agreement ended the Bosnian War at the end of 1995; in 1999 NATO intervened militarily in the Kosovo War without a UN mandate. A UN tribunal in The Hague later convicted many of those responsible.

title: India Opens Its Economy
summary: In a severe balance-of-payments crisis, India opens its state-directed economy to the market and the world market.
text: Since independence India had steered its economy with planning targets, high tariffs and a dense web of state licenses. In 1991 the country faced insolvency because its foreign exchange reserves covered only a few weeks of imports. The government of Prime Minister Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh then lowered tariffs, abolished many licensing requirements and admitted foreign investment. In the following decades the Indian economy grew strongly, especially in software and services around cities such as Bangalore.

title: Treaty of Maastricht
summary: Twelve European states found the European Union and decide on a common currency.
text: On 7 February 1992 the twelve members of the European Community signed a treaty in the Dutch town of Maastricht that raised their cooperation to a new level. When it came into force on 1 November 1993 the European Union was born, meant to cover not only the economy but also foreign, security, justice and home affairs. The treaty introduced citizenship of the Union and laid down the path to economic and monetary union, from which the euro emerged in 1999. In Denmark ratification at first failed in a referendum, and only after exemptions did the Danes approve it in 1993.

title: End of Apartheid and the Election of Mandela
summary: Nelson Mandela is elected president in South Africa's first free elections.
text: From 1948 onward South Africa's white minority had stripped the black majority of its rights and segregated it spatially through the system of apartheid. International sanctions, protests and the resistance of the ANC forced President de Klerk in 1990 to release Mandela and to repeal the racial laws. In April 1994 all South Africans were allowed to vote for the first time; the ANC won, and Mandela became president. A Truth and Reconciliation Commission examined the crimes of apartheid.

title: NAFTA and the Zapatista Uprising
summary: Mexico, the United States and Canada form a free trade area, and on the same day Indigenous rebels rise up in Chiapas.
text: On 1 January 1994 the North American Free Trade Agreement, NAFTA, came into force, gradually removing tariffs between the United States, Canada and Mexico. On the same day the Zapatista Army of National Liberation occupied towns in the southern Mexican state of Chiapas. The predominantly Indigenous fighters protested against poverty, the loss of land and the consequences of free trade for small farmers. After brief fighting the conflict turned into negotiations, and the Zapatistas became a symbol of worldwide criticism of globalization. NAFTA greatly increased trade and was replaced by a new agreement in 2020.

title: Genocide in Rwanda
summary: Within about 100 days Hutu militias murder some 800,000 Tutsi and moderate Hutu while the world looks on.
text: The Belgian colonial power had divided the population of Rwanda into Hutu and Tutsi and favored the Tutsi minority; after independence in 1962 discrimination and violence changed direction. When President Habyarimana's aircraft was shot down on 6 April 1994, the army, militias and incited neighbors began a planned campaign of murder, spurred on by radio stations that described the Tutsi as cockroaches. By July around 800,000 people had been killed with machetes and rifles, many of them in churches and schools to which they had fled. The United Nations even cut its peacekeeping force from about 2,500 to 270. Only the advance of the Tutsi rebels under Paul Kagame brought the killing to an end. An international tribunal later convicted those responsible, and the failure of the world community still shapes the debate about the responsibility to protect.

title: Return of Hong Kong to China
summary: Great Britain hands over its crown colony of Hong Kong to the People's Republic of China after more than 150 years.
text: Hong Kong had been British since the First Opium War and had developed into one of the richest trading and financial cities in Asia. On 1 July 1997 Great Britain handed the colony over to China, which under the principle of one country, two systems guaranteed extensive self-government, a market economy and civil liberties for fifty years. At first Hong Kong remained an open economic center. After large pro-democracy protests in 2019, however, Beijing imposed a national security law in 2020 with which the opposition and the free press were largely suppressed.

title: Vladimir Putin Becomes President of Russia
summary: The former intelligence officer Putin takes power and gradually transforms Russia into an authoritarian state.
text: After years of economic crisis, President Boris Yeltsin unexpectedly resigned on 31 December 1999 and made his prime minister Vladimir Putin acting head of state. Putin, who had made his name with a harsh approach in the Second Chechen War, won the presidential election in March 2000. Thanks to high oil and gas prices incomes rose, and many Russians valued the new stability. At the same time the Kremlin brought the major television channels under its control, persecuted opposition figures and weakened independent courts. A constitutional amendment of 2020 allows Putin to remain in office until 2036.

title: Attacks of 11 September
summary: Islamist terrorists fly hijacked aircraft into the World Trade Center and the Pentagon.
text: On 11 September 2001 nineteen attackers from the terrorist network al-Qaeda hijacked four passenger aircraft. Two brought down the Twin Towers in New York, one struck the Pentagon, and the fourth crashed in Pennsylvania after the passengers resisted. Almost 3,000 people died. The United States declared the war on terror, overthrew the Taliban regime in Afghanistan and invaded Iraq in 2003. Security checks and surveillance changed life all over the world.

title: China Joins the World Trade Organization
summary: By joining the WTO, China finally becomes part of world trade and rises to become the workshop of the world.
text: After fifteen years of negotiations the People's Republic of China became a member of the World Trade Organization on 11 December 2001. It undertook to lower tariffs and open its markets and in return gained access to the markets of the other members. Foreign companies relocated factories to China on a large scale, where millions of migrant workers from the villages produced clothing, electronics and toys for the world market. In 2010 China overtook Japan as the world's second-largest economy. In the United States and Europe, by contrast, many industrial jobs were lost, which later contributed to trade conflicts.

title: War in Afghanistan
summary: After the attacks of 11 September a US-led coalition topples the Taliban, who return to power after twenty years.
text: Because the Taliban government gave shelter to Osama bin Laden and al-Qaeda, the United States and Great Britain began air strikes on Afghanistan in October 2001; by December the regime had fallen. An international security force, led by NATO from 2003 and including the German Bundeswehr, was meant to secure the building of a democratic state. But the Taliban regrouped and waged a long insurgency, while corruption weakened the government in Kabul. After an agreement between the United States and the Taliban, Western troops withdrew in 2021, and on 15 August 2021 the Taliban took Kabul.

title: Introduction of Euro Cash
summary: In twelve EU states euro coins and notes replace the national currencies.
text: The euro had been introduced as book money in 1999; on 1 January 2002 it came into circulation as cash and replaced the deutschmark, the franc, the lira and other currencies. Around 300 million people received a common currency that made trade and travel in Europe easier. The euro crisis from 2010 onward revealed the weaknesses of a currency without a common fiscal policy. Today more than 20 states use the euro.

title: Founding of the African Union
summary: The African states replace the Organization of African Unity with the African Union.
text: The Organization of African Unity, founded in 1963, had supported decolonization but had hardly intervened in the internal affairs of its members, not even during the genocide in Rwanda. In July 2002 the African Union took its place in Durban, South Africa. It may intervene in member states in cases of genocide and serious war crimes and suspends members after military coups. The Union, headquartered in Addis Ababa, comprises 55 states, has sent peacekeeping troops to Somalia, for example, and in 2018 laid the foundation for an African free trade area.

title: Independence of East Timor
summary: After a long Indonesian occupation, East Timor becomes independent as the first new state of the 21st century.
text: The former Portuguese colony of East Timor had been occupied by Indonesia in 1975; in the following decades more than 100,000 people died through violence, hunger and disease. In a vote organized by the United Nations in 1999, almost 80 percent of the population voted for independence. Pro-Indonesian militias then devastated large parts of the country until an international force led by Australia intervened. After a transitional United Nations administration, East Timor became independent on 20 May 2002, with the former resistance leader Xanana Gusmão as its first president.

title: The Human Genome Is Decoded
summary: The international Human Genome Project presents the sequence of the roughly three billion building blocks of human DNA.
text: The Human Genome Project began in 1990 as a collaboration between research institutions in the United States, Great Britain, Japan, France, Germany and China. Its goal was to determine the sequence of the roughly three billion base pairs in the human genome. After a first draft in 2001, the project was completed in April 2003, faster and more cheaply than planned. Among other things it showed that humans have only about 20,000 genes, far fewer than expected. The results form a basis for research into hereditary diseases, for cancer medicine and for genetic testing, but they also raised questions about data protection.

title: Iraq War
summary: A US-led coalition topples Saddam Hussein, but Iraq sinks into insurgency and civil war.
text: The US government under George W. Bush justified the attack on Iraq above all with alleged weapons of mass destruction that were never found. Without a mandate from the UN Security Council and against the opposition of states such as Germany and France, American and British troops invaded in March 2003 and toppled Saddam Hussein within a few weeks. A bloody insurgency and fighting between Shiites and Sunnis followed, in which tens of thousands of civilians died. The United States withdrew its troops in 2011. The so-called Islamic State later emerged from underground groups in Iraq.

title: Eastward Enlargement of the European Union
summary: Ten states, including eight formerly communist countries of Central and Eastern Europe, join the EU.
text: On 1 May 2004 Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Slovenia, Malta and Cyprus joined the European Union. It was the largest enlargement in its history and politically overcame the division of Europe by the Cold War as well. The accession countries had first had to establish democracy, the rule of law and a market economy according to the so-called Copenhagen criteria. Romania and Bulgaria followed in 2007, and Croatia in 2013. The enlargement brought growth and new freedoms, but also disputes over labor migration and the rule of law.

title: Indian Ocean Tsunami
summary: An undersea earthquake off Sumatra triggers a tsunami that kills around 230,000 people in fourteen countries.
text: On 26 December 2004 one of the strongest earthquakes ever measured shook the seabed off the Indonesian island of Sumatra. Within hours the resulting waves struck the coasts of Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand and other countries as far as East Africa. Around 230,000 people died; the Indonesian province of Aceh was hit hardest. People all over the world donated generously for reconstruction. Afterward an early warning system was set up for the Indian Ocean, and in Aceh the disaster contributed to a peace agreement in 2005 after decades of conflict.

title: The Smartphone Conquers the World
summary: Apple presents the iPhone and launches the triumph of the smartphone, which billions of people soon use.
text: On 9 January 2007 Steve Jobs presented the iPhone in San Francisco, a mobile phone with a touch screen, internet access and a music player. From 2008 users could download additional programs from the App Store, and Google's Android operating system brought smartphones from many manufacturers onto the market. Within a few years the devices replaced the camera, the street map, the newspaper and often the computer as well. In Africa and Asia many people went online for the first time on a mobile phone. At the same time concerns grew about data protection, addiction and the power of a few technology companies.

title: Australia's Apology to the Stolen Generations
summary: Prime Minister Kevin Rudd apologizes in parliament for the removal of Indigenous children from their families.
text: For decades Australian authorities and churches had taken Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children from their families in order to raise them in institutions or with white families. An inquiry report of 1997 made the suffering of these Stolen Generations publicly known. On 13 February 2008 Prime Minister Kevin Rudd formally apologized on behalf of parliament and the government. Many Indigenous Australians followed the speech with emotion in parliament and in public squares. The social disadvantage of the Indigenous population nevertheless remained great, and in 2023 voters rejected an Indigenous Voice in the constitution.

title: Election of Barack Obama
summary: With Barack Obama, an African American becomes president of the United States for the first time.
text: In the midst of the global financial crisis, the Democratic senator Barack Obama won the presidential election against the Republican John McCain on 4 November 2008. His election, a little over forty years after the successes of the civil rights movement, was regarded by many as a historic turning point. Obama supported the economy with a large stimulus program and in 2010 pushed through a health care reform that gave millions of Americans health insurance. In 2009 he received the Nobel Peace Prize. His term in office until 2017 was at the same time marked by a sharp political polarization of the country.

title: Global Financial Crisis
summary: The collapse of the bank Lehman Brothers triggers the most severe economic crisis since 1929.
text: American banks had bundled risky mortgage loans into securities and sold them around the world. When property prices fell, the financial system began to totter; on 15 September 2008 Lehman Brothers went bankrupt. Governments rescued banks with hundreds of billions, the world economy contracted, and millions lost their jobs and their homes. The crisis led to stricter banking rules and fed mistrust of elites and of globalization.

title: Arab Spring
summary: Mass protests topple dictators in Tunisia, Egypt and Libya, but in many places lead to war and new repression.
text: The self-immolation of a vegetable seller in Tunisia in December 2010 set off protests against poverty, corruption and oppression that spread through social media across the entire Arab world. In Tunisia and Egypt the presidents resigned, and in Libya Gaddafi was overthrown. In Syria the uprising developed into a civil war with hundreds of thousands dead and millions of refugees. Only Tunisia remained on a democratic path for longer.

title: Civil War in Syria
summary: Peaceful protests against Bashar al-Assad develop into a devastating war with international involvement.
text: In March 2011, in the wake of the Arab Spring, people in Syria too protested against the dictatorship of President Bashar al-Assad. The regime had demonstrators shot, and the uprising turned into a civil war in which rebel groups, Kurds, jihadists of the so-called Islamic State and foreign powers such as Russia, Iran, Turkey and the United States took part. The regime used barrel bombs and poison gas against its own population. Hundreds of thousands of people died, and around half of the population was displaced. In December 2024 rebels overthrew Assad, who fled to Moscow.

title: Earthquake, Tsunami and the Fukushima Nuclear Disaster
summary: An undersea earthquake and a tsunami devastate Japan's northeast coast and cause meltdowns at the Fukushima power plant.
text: On 11 March 2011 an undersea earthquake of magnitude 9 struck off the northeast coast of Japan. A tsunami up to forty meters high destroyed entire coastal towns, and around 18,000 people died or remained missing. At the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant the cooling failed, meltdowns occurred in three reactors, and large amounts of radioactivity were released. More than 100,000 people had to leave their homes. Under the impact of the disaster Germany decided in 2011 on a gradual phase-out of nuclear power, which was completed in 2023.

title: Independence of South Sudan
summary: After decades of civil war, South Sudan breaks away from Sudan and becomes Africa's youngest state.
text: Between the Arab and Muslim north of Sudan and the predominantly Christian and animist south, war raged for decades, from 1955 to 1972 and again from 1983 to 2005. A peace agreement of 2005 provided for a referendum, in which almost 99 percent of South Sudanese voted for independence in January 2011. On 9 July 2011 South Sudan became independent and was admitted to the United Nations as its 193rd member. But as early as 2013 a civil war broke out between supporters of rival politicians, claiming hundreds of thousands of lives and displacing millions of people.

title: China's New Silk Road
summary: Xi Jinping announces a vast infrastructure program intended to link China with Asia, Africa and Europe.
text: In the autumn of 2013 the Chinese state and party leader Xi Jinping presented in Kazakhstan and Indonesia the idea of an economic belt along the old Silk Road and a maritime Silk Road. Under the name Belt and Road Initiative, Chinese banks and firms financed ports, railways, roads and power plants in many countries. For numerous states in Asia and Africa the projects offered urgently needed infrastructure. Critics, however, warned of high debt, a lack of transparency and growing political dependence on China.

title: Ebola Epidemic in West Africa
summary: The largest Ebola epidemic up to that time kills more than 11,000 people in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone.
text: The Ebola virus causes an often fatal fever and is transmitted through bodily fluids. At the end of 2013 an outbreak began in Guinea that spread in 2014 to Liberia and Sierra Leone and for the first time also reached large cities. Weak health systems, distrust of the authorities and traditional burial rites made it harder to fight. In total around 28,000 people fell ill and more than 11,000 died. The World Health Organization was criticized for its late response, and the experience contributed to the development of an Ebola vaccine.

title: Russia Annexes Crimea
summary: After the fall of the pro-Russian Ukrainian president, Russia occupies Crimea and fuels the war in the Donbas.
text: In the winter of 2013/14 hundreds of thousands of people protested on the Maidan in Kyiv against President Viktor Yanukovych, who had halted an agreement with the EU under pressure from Moscow. After bloody clashes Yanukovych fled to Russia in February 2014. Shortly afterward Russian soldiers without insignia occupied the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, and after a referendum that was not recognized internationally Russia incorporated it in March 2014. In eastern Ukraine a war began between Ukrainian troops and separatists supported by Russia. The EU and the United States imposed sanctions on Russia.

title: Refugee Movement to Europe
summary: More than a million people, above all from Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq, seek protection in Europe.
text: Because of the wars in Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq and poor conditions in the refugee camps of neighboring countries, hundreds of thousands set out for Europe in 2015. Many came via Turkey and the Greek islands and moved on north along the so-called Balkan route; thousands drowned in the Mediterranean. In September 2015 the German government under Angela Merkel decided to let refugees stranded in Hungary enter the country. In 2015 more than 1.2 million asylum applications were filed in the EU. The dispute over distribution, border protection and integration divided the EU and strengthened right-wing populist parties.

title: Paris Climate Agreement
summary: Almost all states of the world commit themselves to limiting global warming to well below two degrees.
text: At the world climate conference in Paris on 12 December 2015, almost all the states of the Earth agreed on a new climate agreement. It sets the goal of limiting warming compared with pre-industrial times to well below two degrees and of keeping it to 1.5 degrees if possible. Unlike the Kyoto Protocol of 1997, it also obliges emerging and developing countries to set their own climate targets and to tighten them regularly. The United States withdrew under President Donald Trump, rejoined in 2021 and announced its withdrawal again in 2025. According to scientific assessments, the commitments made by states so far are not yet sufficient to reach the goals.

title: Brexit: Great Britain Leaves the EU
summary: In a referendum a narrow majority of the British vote to leave the European Union.
text: On 23 June 2016 Prime Minister David Cameron held a referendum on Great Britain's membership of the EU, and 51.9 percent of voters chose to leave. Supporters wanted to regain control over laws, borders and immigration, while opponents warned of economic damage. Scotland and Northern Ireland voted by a majority to remain. After years of negotiations, above all over the border between Ireland and Northern Ireland, Great Britain left the EU on 31 January 2020. It was the first time a member state had left the Union.

title: Peace Agreement in Colombia
summary: The Colombian government and the FARC guerrillas end one of the longest armed conflicts in the world.
text: Since 1964 the left-wing FARC guerrillas had fought against the Colombian state; the conflict, in which right-wing paramilitaries and drug cartels were also involved, cost hundreds of thousands of people their lives and displaced millions. After four years of negotiations in Havana, President Juan Manuel Santos and the FARC concluded a peace agreement in 2016. When the population narrowly rejected it in October, it was revised and approved by parliament in November. Santos received the Nobel Peace Prize, and around 13,000 FARC fighters and supporters laid down their arms. Implementation remained difficult because other armed groups continued to fight.

title: The MeToo Movement
summary: Under the slogan MeToo, millions of women make sexual harassment and violence public.
text: In October 2017 American newspapers reported on decades of sexual assaults by the Hollywood producer Harvey Weinstein. Thereupon the actress Alyssa Milano called on those affected to share their experiences under the phrase MeToo, which the activist Tarana Burke had coined as early as 2006. Within a few days millions of people in many countries used the hashtag on social media. Powerful men in film, media, politics and business lost their positions, and Weinstein was later convicted. The movement sparked debates worldwide about abuse of power and equality in the workplace.

title: Christchurch Attack
summary: A far-right terrorist kills 51 people in two mosques in New Zealand.
text: On 15 March 2019 an Australian right-wing extremist attacked two mosques in the New Zealand city of Christchurch during Friday prayers and killed 51 people. He livestreamed the attack on the internet and had previously circulated a racist manifesto. Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern showed solidarity with the Muslim victims and within a few weeks had military-style semi-automatic weapons banned. Together with France she launched an international initiative against terrorist content online. In 2020 the perpetrator became the first person in New Zealand to be sentenced to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

title: COVID-19 Pandemic
summary: A novel coronavirus spreads across the world; lockdowns and vaccination campaigns shape two years.
text: At the end of 2019 the virus SARS-CoV-2 appeared in the Chinese city of Wuhan; in March 2020 the World Health Organization declared a pandemic. Governments closed schools, shops and borders, public life came to a temporary standstill, and working from home and video conferences became part of everyday life. Within a year vaccines were developed and billions of doses were administered worldwide. According to WHO estimates, around 20 million people died of or with COVID-19 by 2023.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Becomes Part of Everyday Life
summary: With ChatGPT, an artificial intelligence language program is used by millions of people within a few months.
text: On 30 November 2022 the US company OpenAI released the dialogue program ChatGPT, which is based on a large language model. Such models are trained on vast amounts of text and can write texts, answer questions, translate and generate program code. ChatGPT gained more than a hundred million users within a short time, and competitors in the United States, China and Europe brought out similar systems. Schools, universities and companies had to find new rules, and experts debated misinformation, copyright and the consequences for jobs. In 2024 the EU became the first major economic power to adopt a comprehensive law regulating artificial intelligence.

title: Russian Attack on Ukraine
summary: On 24 February 2022 Russia invades Ukraine and begins the largest war in Europe since 1945.
text: After the annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the war in the Donbas, President Vladimir Putin ordered the attack on the whole of the neighboring country on 24 February 2022, a country he regards as part of Russia and wanted to remove from the sphere of influence of the West. The swift victory he expected did not come about: the Ukrainian army and population defended Kyiv, and when the Russians withdrew, massacres of civilians were discovered in Bucha and other places. The Western states imposed unprecedented sanctions and supplied weapons, Finland and Sweden joined NATO, and millions of Ukrainians fled to Europe. With hundreds of thousands killed and wounded, cities destroyed and energy and food prices rising worldwide, the war put an end to hopes of a lasting peaceful order in Europe.

title: Hamas Attack on Israel and War in Gaza
summary: After the Hamas terrorist attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, Israel wages a devastating war in the Gaza Strip.
text: On 7 October 2023 fighters of Hamas and other groups broke into Israel from the Gaza Strip, killed around 1,200 people, most of them civilians, and abducted about 250 hostages. It was the day on which the most Jews were killed since the Holocaust. Israel responded with an air and ground offensive that destroyed large parts of the Gaza Strip; tens of thousands of Palestinians were killed, and almost the entire population was displaced and suffered from hunger. The war expanded to Lebanon and to confrontations with Iran. International courts dealt with accusations of war crimes, and a ceasefire agreed in January 2025 held only until March 2025.
